item.title: Trump backs Elon Musk in latest MAGA breakup
item.description:
President Trump still considers Elon Musk an ally despite the world's richest man saying he's "not MAGA," the president told NBC News on Thursday.

Why it matters: Musk's latest break from Trump's political movement comes after he spent millions backing Republicans in the midterms, only to see Democrats win control of Congress and many state governments.

  • Trump and Musk have weathered public feuds before, repeatedly reconciling despite disagreements.

Driving the news: "He's a friend of mine," Trump told NBC News of Musk.

  • "There are lots of definitions out there. MAGA, to me, means something very specific, and when people veer from it, they don't do very well," Trump said.
  • "Elon's got very good intentions," he said. "I mean, he was with me the whole — he traveled with me."

Catch up quick: Musk said at the The New York Times' DealBook Summit Wednesday that he considers himself politically moderate.

  • "I'm not sure what MAGA means, but if that means sort of blind adherence to a set of policies by the Republican Party, then I certainly don't have that," Musk told the New York Times.
  • Musk said he felt "pretty foolish" about spending millions in the midterms.
  • "If I could rewind the clock, I would have spent less money," he said.

Yes, but: Musk reportedly accompanied Trump to China this week, underscoring how their personal relationship has endured despite their political differences.

Between the lines: Musk may reject the MAGA label, but he has spent years championing its culture wars, bankrolling Republicans and turning X, the social media platform he bought for $44 billion, into a megaphone for far-right voices.

  • He has attacked diversity initiatives, amplified anti-immigration rhetoric and promoted an antisemitic conspiracy theory for which he later apologized.
  • He has also railed against what he calls the "woke mind virus" and backed far-right political movements abroad.

Flashback: Musk has clashed with Trump over government spending, tariffs, climate policy and the investigation into Jeffrey Epstein.

  • In October 2024, Musk joked at a Trump rally, "I'm not just MAGA, I'm dark MAGA."
  • Despite their disagreements, Musk has repeatedly reentered Trump's orbit.

What we're watching: Sen. Ruben Gallego (D-Ariz.) and Rep. Yassamin Ansari (D-Ariz.) suggested the tech mogul could still face Congressional probes once Democrats take office next year regardless of whether he breaks with MAGA.

item.title: Meta rethinks climate goal as AI emissions soar 45%
item.description:
Meta's greenhouse gas emissions surged 45% last year amid its AI infrastructure boom, prompting the tech giant to reconsider its goal of reaching net-zero emissions by 2030.

Why it matters: Other tech giants have reported rising emissions as they race to build data centers, but Meta is going a step further by explicitly reconsidering its climate deadline.

Driving the news: The just-released sustainability report of the tech giant, one of North America's largest data centers operators, shows just how much growth in the AI industry is outpacing any efficiency gains.

  • Meta executives said they were "re-evaluating" the 2030 goal, first announced in 2020 when the company was still known as Facebook and before the generative AI boom.
  • They didn't specify what changes they're considering or when they'll make a decision.

By the numbers: Meta's electricity use jumped 35%, comparable to other tech giants. But Meta's emissions increase of 45% is far higher than its peers, Google (18%), Amazon (16%) and Microsoft (25%).

What they're saying: "When we set our net zero emissions goal, we anticipated steady growth, falling clean energy costs, and changes in the broader system that would enable progress at the pace we envisioned," wrote Rachel Peterson, vice president of data centers, and Blair Swedeen, global head of net zero and sustainability.

  • "The reality has been far more complex."

Zoom out: The race among tech giants to dominate AI is pushing their climate goals into the backseat, even as they continue investing heavily in clean energy.

State of play: Meta says it has contracted more than 30 gigawatts of clean energy, including nuclear, solar and geothermal, though less than half that capacity is generating electricity so far.

The intrigue: Meta's report says it may turn to natural gas plants to power data centers when utilities can't deliver electricity fast enough — even though such projects are already underway.

  • It's also seeking to offset some of the methane emissions associated with its natural gas use by paying for cleaner gas production elsewhere.

Reality check: Meta's 45% emissions increase doesn't yet reflect the full impact of some of its biggest planned natural gas projects, suggesting its footprint could grow considerably more.

  • In Louisiana, utility Entergy is pursuing seven new gas-fired generating units totaling more than 5,200 megawatts to serve Meta's data centers.
  • Separately, Ohio regulators approved a 200-megawatt gas plant built specifically to power Meta's data centers, while research firm Cleanview identifies a 521-megawatt gas project under construction for Meta in Utah.

Friction point: Meta's report was also revealing about water, a more immediate concern for many communities near data centers.

  • The company's direct water consumption fell 4%, but consumption in highly water-stressed regions rose 24%.
  • The estimated water consumption associated with generating its electricity — an often-overlooked environmental impact — rose 37% before accounting for its clean-energy purchases.

How it works: Natural gas plants typically use substantial amounts of water for cooling, meaning Meta's growing reliance on gas could increase its indirect water footprint even as its data centers become more water-efficient.

Yes, but: Meta is the only tech giant to disclose the water consumption associated with electricity, earning it high marks for transparency from Alex de Vries-Gao, a researcher at Vrije Universiteit Amsterdam who has studied AI's environmental footprint.

What we're watching: Meta's reconsideration of its climate deadline raises the question of whether other tech giants will eventually follow suit as the AI boom continues to strain their environmental commitments.

item.title: Myanmar becomes first state found responsible for genocide by UN court
item.description:
Myanmar became the first state the International Court of Justice has held responsible for committing genocide in a landmark ruling Thursday.

Why it matters: The decision could have far-reaching implications for other genocide cases, including South Africa's case accusing Israel of committing genocide against Palestinians in Gaza.

State of play: The court ruled 9–6 that Myanmar's violent 2017 military crackdown was intended to destroy the country's persecuted Rohingya Muslim minority.

  • The onslaught killed thousands and forced more than 740,000 Rohingya to flee to neighboring Bangladesh.
  • In 2021, Myanmar's military coup also sparked a civil war that killed over 100,000 people and displaced 5.2 million, according to the Council on Foreign Relation's Global Conflict Tracker.
  • Myanmar has repeatedly denied allegations of mass rape, murder and arson.

Yes, but: The legally binding ruling does not guarantee that the roughly 1.2 million Rohingya refugees in Bangladesh will be able to safely return home.

  • The court ordered Myanmar to investigate and punish those responsible, provide reparations to the Rohingya and allow refugees to return.
  • Still, the ICJ has no direct way to enforce its ruling.

What they're saying: "This judgment must now translate into real action," UN Human Rights Chief Volker Türk said in a statement.

  • "The Court has made clear Myanmar's responsibilities. It sends a strong message to all States around the world that those responsible for genocide will be held to account."
  • Myanmar's opposition National Unity Government welcomed the ruling, saying it would "carefully consider the Court's findings and any orders issued" and remained committed to holding perpetrators accountable and preventing further atrocities.

Flashback: In 2022, the Biden administration formally declared that Myanmar's military committed genocide against the country's Rohingya minority and crimes against humanity.

  • The ICJ in 2020 ordered Myanmar to protect Rohingya from genocide while the case was pending.

Go deeper: UN court rejects Myanmar's objections to Rohingya genocide case

item.title: Why the Senate energy permitting bill might become law
item.description:
If the sweeping Senate permitting bill becomes law, it will reflect a rare convergence of political and market forces strong enough to trump the Beltway aversion to big, bipartisan deals.

Why it matters: The bill could transform how America builds energy infrastructure, with major implications for everything from electricity costs to data centers.

  • Getting rid of bureaucratic hurdles for energy projects is a top priority for the fossil fuels and renewables sectors.
  • But critics argue the plan would unacceptably weaken environmental protections and the rights of Native American tribes.

The latest: A vote on final passage of the White House-backed bill could occur Thursday after the Senate plows through some more amendments.

The big picture: Many industries — pipelines, transmission, housing, you name it — call permitting a long bureaucratic and judicial maze that stymies projects.

Yes, but: That, on its own, isn't nearly enough to get this far. Here are other reasons the bill has a path to becoming law after years of failed efforts to upend permitting.

🗳️ The cost-of-living election. The midterms were soaked in affordability politics at a time of rising energy bills.

  • While critics can call the projected savings modest, cost is politically front and center.
  • The Rhodium Group estimates that big provisions it analyzed would cut average residential power prices by 3%-4% in 2035. Third Way, a group that favors the bill, supported the research firm's work.

📈 Rising electricity demand. U.S. power thirst has been rising in the last few years after staying largely flat for decades, driven partly by AI and wider electrification of the economy.

🦋 A maturing clean energy industry. As sectors like renewables and storage become more mainstream, "more developers and companies are seeing the real-world challenges" of doing projects, clean energy lobbyist Jeff Navin notes via email.

  • That puts them in agreement with utilities and oil and gas companies. "They all run into problems getting the permits needed to build energy infrastructure," said Navin, an Obama-era Energy Department aide and former Democratic Capitol Hill staff member.
  • Easier permitting is needed for transmission to carry the industries' power, as well as for building new generation itself.

😣 A mercurial White House was focused. The White House's National Energy Dominance Council was engaged with the bill.

  • Co-author Shelly Moore Capito (R-W.Va.) credited then-chief of staff Susie Wiles as a helpful player at the Sept. 30 bill rollout. Axios' Alex Isenstadt reported that new chief of staff Stephen Miller also wants a permitting bill.
  • Trump officials have also allowed some onshore wind projects bottled up by Pentagon reviews to proceed.

🔀 Shifting Democratic coalitions. Multiple analyses show the bill bringing somewhat lower power sector emissions compared to a world without it.

  • But when climate had more political juice a few years ago, a bill backed by oil industry groups probably would not have had this much Democratic buy-in.
  • Democratic co-authors and other supporters in the Dem coalition say easing the clean energy buildout is key to more climate progress in the future.
  • More moderate center-left voices and think tanks have new cachet, while environmental groups opposing the bill haven't made enough inroads despite longstanding ties to Democrats.

The intrigue: Data centers have been and remain a wildcard. There's a big political and public backlash, and opponents of the bill have seized on it, charging that the bill would help Big Tech by making the buildout easier.

  • But bill authors and backers are emphasizing language designed to ensure that data centers pay for grid upgrades and have higher transmission service costs.

What we're watching: The House. If it can pass the bill before the end of the year, there's a good chance the bill will get signed into law. If not, it's just another failed effort.

Sign up here for Axios' Future of Energy newsletter.

item.title: New alarm over China controlling drug supply chains
item.description:
China is intensifying efforts to control the entire drug supply chain, putting the U.S. at risk of being cut off from future lifesaving treatments, the National Security Commission on Emerging Biotechnology warns in a new analysis out Thursday.

Why it matters: Western drug giants have invested huge sums in Chinese biotechs to boost their product pipelines. But sharing capital and expertise could give Beijing more control over critical pharmaceutical technologies.

  • Concerns about the U.S. getting boxed out have intensified after the Chinese government proposed new restrictions last month on the export of certain technologies, including cell and gene therapy platforms.

Driving the news: Western drug giants are increasingly entering into licensing agreements with Chinese firms that redirect U.S. capital away from U.S. innovation and toward the Chinese pharmaceutical industry, the commission found in its analysis of 57 deals from the beginning of 2023 through last month.

  • The deals are being made earlier in the drug discovery process, allowing the Chinese partners to gain not just capital but know-how in developing and commercializing treatments.
  • This kind of knowledge transfer in automobiles, semiconductors and industrial chemicals gave Chinese industry a competitive edge and leverage to control global markets for the products, according to the commission, which was established by Congress to examine how emerging biotech intersects with national security.
  • "The end game is the same for the [Chinese Communist Party] in the pharmaceutical industry," the commission warns, saying the goal is increased U.S. dependence on Chinese innovation and enrichment of the Chinese pharmaceutical industry.

Between the lines: Drugmakers including AstraZeneca, Bristol Myers Squibb and Pfizer have been drawn by China's surge of investment in the life sciences and the promise of faster clinical trials and product approvals.

  • Typically a Chinese biotechnology company sells the license to develop or commercialize a treatment it developed to a multinational pharmaceutical company.
  • The Western companies see the arrangements as a way to outsource the burden of drug discovery and verify early results. But the commission found that the deals are increasingly based on preclinical data and that upfront payments are coming earlier in the R&D cycle.
  • The commission says this can result in a "flywheel effect" that sees royalties and equity in joint ventures flow back to China, fueling new research and infrastructure and attracting global talent.

What they're saying: "The CCP seeks dominance in biotechnology as a source of economic power and geopolitical advantage, and Beijing has spent decades pursuing a deliberate strategy to achieve that at all levels of the value chain," said commission executive director Caitlin Frazer.

  • "U.S.-China pharma deals are starting to favor the Chinese startups, which risks eroding biotech R&D in the U.S. This trend should be alarming for policymakers."

Threat level: The concern is what happens if China scales up and corners a market, establishing a stranglehold on supplies of key products and ingredients.

  • That's especially critical in pharma. While a chip shortage may result in delays replacing a car or phone, a drug shortage delays treatments for controlling seizures, treating infections or managing severe pain, Brookings Institution senior fellow Marta Wosińska has noted.
  • In a report last year to Congress, the commission posed a hypothetical scenario in which Beijing withheld a breakthrough treatment from American patients in the event of a conflict in Taiwan.

State of play: Last month, the Trump administration proposed subjecting certain deals with Chinese life sciences companies to new screening requirements or prohibiting them altogether.

  • The administration cited the risk of "outbound investments" being used to create biological weapons or brain-computer interfaces for surveillance, or to make U.S. supply chains overly dependent on a country.
  • Cash-based deals that bring royalties and milestone payments are still permitted, but equity investments in Chinese firms would be prohibited and certain joint ventures could also be targeted, per a Sidley analysis.

The commission, in its new analysis, calls the proposal "a prudent step to curtail China's biotechnology ambitions" but adds policymakers "must act now to empower the United States to out-innovate strategic competitors before it's too late."

  • Pharma and biotech interests have been pressing Congress and the administration to take steps to update and streamline U.S. drug development, improve patient access to clinical trials and pass stronger patent protections.

What we're watching: Whether this week's meetings between President Trump and China's Xi Jinping yield new agreements on strategic technologies like biotech or lead to tighter export controls.

item.title: Poll: Republicans in early 2028 primary states back Israel, not its critics
item.description:
Republican voters in four early 2028 primary states have favorable views of Israel by wide margins and have negative opinions of three leading right-wing critics of the Jewish state, according to a new poll by a national GOP consulting firm.

Why it matters: The poll challenges the notion that Republican opinion toward Israel is fracturing significantly, and points to a potential disconnect between GOP voters' attitudes and the sentiments of those who often draw the most attention online.

  • The survey, conducted by OnMessage Inc. for the Combat Antisemitism Movement's political arm, essentially provides a roadmap for pro-Israel Republicans' messaging ahead of the 2028 presidential campaign.
  • It seeks to cast the right's leading critics of Israel — Tucker Carlson, Candace Owens and Nick Fuentes — as liabilities in the GOP primary.

Zoom in: After the midterms, Vice President Vance called on the U.S. and the GOP to "change our relationship to Israel," elevating the nations' longtime partnership as a 2028 campaign issue at a time when Vance is eyeing a presidential bid.

  • Israel is supported by 68% of Republican voters in Iowa, New Hampshire, Nevada and South Carolina, according to the survey, a result similar to findings by Gallup and Pew. 17% disfavored Israel.
  • 78% said the GOP's "relationship with Israel" makes them more likely to vote Republican. Large majorities also agreed with pro-Israel messages.

In contrast, 53% of those surveyed said they disapprove of Carlson, and 30% approve. But among voters under 45 years old, Carlson's approval/disproval ratings were tied at 46%.

  • 49% of the Republicans surveyed disapproved of Owens, while 23% approved.
  • Fuentes, the least-known of the three media figures, was viewed unfavorably by 25% and favored by 13%. Among self-described MAGA Republicans, 22% approved and 23% disapproved of him, however.
  • "The fringe messengers are underwater," says a slide deck for the poll, which was conducted ahead of the Combat Antisemitism Movement's national conference Thursday in Charleston, S.C.

Stunning stat: Vance is more popular in the GOP than President Trump.

  • 75% view Trump favorably and 23% disfavor him, a net of +52 points.
  • Vance: 80% favorable and 19% unfavorable, a net of +61.
  • Another bright spot for Vance —59% agreed with this statement, which generally reflects the vice president's position: "Israel has a right to exist, and America should remain its ally, however criticism of its government is legitimate, but when it turns into antisemitism that is unacceptable."

The intrigue: Vance is friends with Carlson, whose son used to work in the vice president's office. The two have resisted speaking ill of each other even as Carlson has grown more critical of the president and the war in Iran.

  • 46% of the GOP voters surveyed said a Carlson endorsement of a presidential candidate would make them less likely to support that person; 16% said it would make them more likely and 39% said it wouldn't matter.

Yes, but: The poll is conducted for an advocacy group and seeks to provide messaging guidance for candidates and surrogates. So some of its questions are leading.

  • By 83%-5%, Republicans said they viewed Carlson less favorably when told "he endorsed Democrat Abdul El-Sayed, a radical Muslim socialist recently elected to the U.S. Senate in Michigan whose political associates include someone that said, 'America deserved 9/11.' "
  • The survey tested ways to attack Owens and Fuentes on the campaign trail by describing extreme comments from both and found that outsized majorities of Republican voters would call on a candidate to denounce them.
  • By 86%-7%, respondents agreed with the statement, "There is no place for antisemitism in the Republican Party." And 66% said there's no place in the party for antisemites, while 15% said they should be welcomed under a "big tent."

What they're saying: Fuentes declined to comment, Owens couldn't be reached and Carlson questioned the financiers of the poll.

  • "The poll was commissioned by the 'Combat Antisemitism Movement'? Seriously? Pretty funny. Where does their funding come from?" Carlson asked via text. (The donors are primarily Jewish and Zionist contributors, according to Influence Watch).
  • "If the point is to convince Republican candidates that American voters love [Israeli leader Benjamin] Netanyahu and want more wars for Israel, good luck in the next election," he said. "It's so absurd. But I'm sure you'll have Republican senators waving around the poll results like they mean something."
  • Former Virginia Attorney General Jason Miyares, a U.S. Advisory Board Member of the Combat Antisemitism Movement, dismissed the criticism: "For a Republican presidential candidate, standing up against antisemitism is not a political risk — it is the price of admission and good politics. Most importantly, it is simply the right thing to do."

The poll of 1,000 respondents (250 from each of the four early states) was conducted Nov. 7-10. The margin of error: +/- 3.1%.

item.title: Putting cyber risk in perspective, from the experts (our own CTO)
item.description:
Axios chief technology officer Dan Cox, who's spent 25 years at some of the world's biggest tech companies, puts the recent spate of high-profile failures in perspective:

My parents, my siblings and plenty of other people are asking the same question: How worried should we be?

The big picture: I've been in technology a long time. I take these threats seriously, but I'm not in panic mode.

  • When something breaks, we need to understand what happened, how far it reaches and what we can do about it.
  • A frightening headline doesn't answer those questions.

Zoom out: The way I think about it, we've put powerful tools in more hands, and people are taking potshots to see what they can hit. Those shots can do real damage, and we need to protect ourselves.

  • But hearing gunfire doesn't, by itself, mean an army is coming over the hill.
  • We need to understand who's firing, what they can actually do and whether the threat is changing.

Zoom in: Over the past few weeks, we've identified bad actors snooping around our own website, too. Our talented engineers have investigated threats and put mitigations in place.

  • There may still be attempts on our site, but each incident gives us an opportunity to strengthen our systems.

Between the lines: There are thousands of smart, resourceful and dedicated engineers working to protect the systems we all rely on. I see that commitment in our own team.

  • I believe that if the threat grows, more people with those skills will step up. That's part of why I have confidence in our ability to respond, even as the threats evolve.

The bottom line: Fred Rogers shared his mother's advice for frightening news: "Look for the helpers. You will always find people who are helping."

  • I think about that here. There are a lot of capable people working on these problems. I have confidence in them, even while we have real work to do.
  • I want people to feel informed enough to act, rather than frightened enough to assume the worst.

item.title: Doomsday prepping goes mainstream
item.description:
The internet has caught the emergency preparation bug, fueled by fears of AI-led cyberattacks, power grid vulnerabilities, transportation standstills and international threats.

The big picture: The "prepper" mindset is resonating with larger slices of society — who are packing emergency bags, stocking up on water and taking inventory of non-perishables.

  • Michael Mills, a University of Greenwich senior lecturer who studies doomsday preparation, says some people are turning to "lightweight versions" of traditional prepping amid doubts about global stability.

By the numbers: Sales at Survival Frog, a survival retailer that sells gear like emergency food and radios, saw sales jump 450% between Oct. 27 and Nov. 16, compared to prior weeks, CEO and founder Byron Walker tells Axios.

  • Competitors saw similar trends, he says. And most recent buyers at Survival Frog were new customers.
  • Food, including canned meats, leads demand, Walker says, followed by products like radios, solar generators, battery packs and water filters.

State of play: Systems the world relies on for travel, communications, business, food, health care and more have been disrupted in recent weeks — whether because of tech shortfalls or malicious acts.

  • While officials assure the incidents aren't broadly connected, fears of critical infrastructure failing are growing, and more people considering how to prepare for crises.
  • "It does seem much more mainstream now," Walker says of preppers. "You can't turn on the news without hearing about a new cyber attack or a tech meltdown."
  • Many of the emergency preparation skills people are using have long been observed in disaster-prone areas. And as many Americans learned during COVID, supply chain disruptions mean having extra water, radios and shelf-stable foods around the house isn't a bad thing.

Krystal, known online as the "Queen of Doomsday," spends about five hours daily coaching new preppers and told Axios that recent online engagement with her content, which she says has more than doubled across platforms, has been "mind-blowing."

  • "Families are generally concerned —...people who would have normally turned their nose away from it and thought, 'No, nothing could ever happen.' We've seen lockdowns. We've seen supply chains be crippled. We've seen oil crises, inflation," she says.

Between the lines: Overlapping tech oddities boosted "a sense of anxiety about social stability around us, knowing that planes can be grounded, or fridges can all of a sudden become heaters," Mills says.

  • Costco has become an apparent cornucopia for concerned consumers, with sales on goods like rice, canned goods and water reportedly surging.

Walker attributes the Survival Frog sales boom to the U.K. government and EU urging households to prepare three days of supplies, as well as the Pentagon readiness plan for military bases to operate at least 90 days, per Fox reporting, if civilian systems fail.

  • That plan fueled rumors about a 90-day "blackout" across the U.S.

Worth noting: Asked about the outages and Pentagon preparations, Vice President JD Vance told Fox News' Laura Ingraham that friends have asked whether they should be "preparing to build a bunker" or stock up on food and water.

  • "And my answer to that is no," he continued. "We do not see some crisis coming down."

The bottom line: But Krystal said in a video response to Vance, "Yes, we should be preparing."

  • She's not here to fear-monger, but she tells Axios, "one more person prepared is one less person to worry about if there's a crisis."

Go deeper: The internet's latest obsession: The end of the world

item.title: AI's great divergence: Machines accelerate as makers unravel
item.description:
Anthropic will make its Wall Street debut Thursday at a moment of profound contradiction in the history of AI:

  • The humans are embattled — bogged down by scandal, financial turmoil and political revolt.
  • But the machines are ascendant — accelerating toward an "intelligence explosion" they expect will transform civilization.

Why it matters: The industry's recent chaos has obscured a breathtaking surge in technological progress, forcing some of the world's leading researchers to reconsider just how soon AI could surpass human intelligence.

Zoom in: Inside Anthropic, soon to be valued north of $1 trillion, independent researchers at METR found that AI models are advancing at nearly twice their historical pace — largely fueled, they believe, by AI itself.

  • Anthropic's own data shows Claude went from leading fewer than 1% of the company's AI research tasks in February to more than a quarter by August, with humans still supervising.
  • METR found no clear obstacles to sustaining this pace over the next year, and reviewed confidential evidence suggesting the acceleration itself may be gathering speed.

Zoom out: Across the frontier, leading companies are racing up what Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei calls "the exponential."

  • OpenAI disclosed Tuesday that Astra 6.2 is its first publicly released model to reach the "High" threshold for AI self-improvement — equivalent, the company says, to giving every researcher another highly capable engineer.
  • The advances span both software and silicon: OpenAI says its models helped AMD compress a year of chip-design progress into less than five months, while Google's Gemini is reducing weeks of chip-layout work to hours.

The big picture: These breakthroughs are pushing some of AI's top forecasters to shorten their timelines for the fabled "intelligence explosion" — a runaway cascade of self-improving AI that could propel machine intelligence far beyond human comprehension.

  • The influential AI Futures Project now expects machines to surpass the world's best human AI researchers next year, a dramatic revision driven largely by METR's findings at Anthropic.
  • Paul Christiano, an AI safety pioneer who recently joined OpenAI's board, puts the odds of superintelligence emerging within a year at one in three if development continues at its current pace.

Between the lines: For all their extraordinary capabilities, the machines remain at the mercy of a fallible human race.

  • Take Nvidia: Jensen Huang's sex scandal has plunged the chipmaker into crisis at the very height of its technological and financial power, endangering virtually the entire AI ecosystem.
  • AI leaders' disastrous messaging, veering between promises of utopia and warnings of mass unemployment, has poisoned public trust and helped fuel a revolt against data centers.

Meanwhile, the industry's enormous capital requirements, increasingly tangled financial arrangements and intensifying U.S.–China chip war threaten to impose limits that the technology itself has yet to encounter.

  • Then there's the question of control: Months after OpenAI's agents breached Hugging Face, the company acknowledged Wednesday that it still cannot fully rely on AI behaving as intended to prevent harm.
  • One of the industry's biggest gambles is that AI itself will help solve the problem of controlling future superintelligence. "You're building the plane as you fly it," Christiano told podcaster Dwarkesh Patel this week.

The bottom line: Anthropic's historic IPO captures the central contradiction: Investors are betting on nearly limitless technological progress, while the industry's future remains hostage to distinctly human failures.

item.title: Exclusive: Bots amplified conspiracy theories and panic about recent tech outages
item.description:
Bot accounts have helped spread conspiracy theories about a wave of major tech outages over the last week, according to new research shared exclusively with Axios.

Why it matters: Purveyors of disinformation appear to be exploiting public anxiety over the cyberattacks and fragile infrastructure, amplifying suspicions of coordinated cyberattacks and government cover-ups.

  • While it's unclear who's behind these accounts, the pattern shows that when technology failures lack substantive explanations, bot networks will fill the void to manufacture panic.

Catch up quick: Microsoft, Apple, JPMorgan Chase, United, Workday, the Federal Aviation Administration and the National Security Agency each faced outages over the last week.

  • Then came the conspiracy theories: When the FAA grounded flights for four hours Friday, people were quick to assume it was tied to the rollout of an AI tool at the agency. Some also tried linking the widespread Microsoft outage to recent company layoffs.

Yes, but: There's no publicly established evidence that these outages were part of a coordinated cyberattack, despite the theories circulating online.

  • Several companies have attributed their disruptions to technical problems, rather than malicious activity, including efforts to patch vulnerabilities in order to make software more resilient.
  • Downdetector data show that while the seven days through Monday saw the highest number of weekly outages in the last 12 months, longer-term patterns are far from unprecedented, as Axios previously reported.

By the numbers: Suspected bots accounted for roughly 30% of posts promoting conspiracy theories about several recent tech outages, according to data from social media monitoring firm PeakMetrics.

  • During Microsoft's outage, bots accounted for 26% of conspiratorial posts.
  • Bots accounted for 34% of conspiracy-related posts during Friday's Workday outage, compared with 27% of other posts.
  • Likely bot accounts also made up 31% of conspiracy-related posts about Bank of America's outage and 28% of posts linking Chase's outage to other disruptions.
  • PeakMetrics analyzed social media discussions surrounding six recent outages and automatically classification accounts that were likely to be bots and conspiracy-related posts.

Threat level: Jessica Pratt, a spokesperson for PeakMetrics, told Axios that most of the bot activity is aimed at "gaming the platforms' algorithms" and that they see some foreign influence within that — although the company could not detail precisely how many of the bots are tied to foreign state media and governments.

  • PeakMetrics also observed a "small number of foreign state media and state-aligned accounts in the conversation," Pratt added.

Zoom in: The most popular theory being pushed was that each of these incidents must be connected.

  • More than half of posts about Chase's outage linked it to other recent disruptions, including the FAA ground stop and Microsoft's outage.
  • A fabricated statement attributed to JPMorgan Chase CEO Jamie Dimon fueled speculation that North Korean and Russian hackers were behind the banking outages.
  • During Microsoft's outage, suspected bots circulated identical posts linking the disruption to Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's departure and banking outages in Japan and Paraguay.

The big picture: Foreign influence operations have historically used bots to amplify political grievances and spread false narratives, but it's unclear who's operating the accounts pushing theories about the latest outages.

Between the lines: The longer outages dragged on without clear explanations, the more room conspiracy theories had to spread.

  • During Microsoft's outage, speculative posts nearly tripled on the second day, when the disruption had stretched beyond 12 hours.
  • By then, nearly one in five posts offered an alternative explanation for the outage, according to PeakMetrics.

The intrigue: Questions about whether the outages are connected have also reached Washington, where senior officials and lawmakers are raising concerns about what might be causing the disruptions.

  • House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries told reporters Tuesday that "it's unclear if (the outages are) all infrastructure related or whether there's some malignant activity." Jeffries said he wants briefings for lawmakers in both chambers.
  • Sen. Josh Hawley (R-Mo.) told reporters that it would be "the greatest coincidence in the history of the world" if these outages aren't connected, according to NBC News.

What to watch: Outages are about to become the new normal as organizations race to patch critical vulnerabilities discovered by AI before hackers can use AI to weaponize them.

  • During Microsoft's outage, speculative posts nearly tripled on the second day, when the disruption had stretched beyond 12 hours.
  • By then, nearly one in five posts offered an alternative explanation for the outage, according to PeakMetrics.

The intrigue: Questions about whether the outages are connected have also reached Washington, where senior officials and lawmakers are raising concerns about what might be causing the disruptions.

  • House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries told reporters Tuesday that "it's unclear if (the outages are) all infrastructure related or whether there's some malignant activity." Jeffries said he wants briefings for lawmakers in both chambers.
  • Sen. Josh Hawley (R-Mo.) told reporters that it would be "the greatest coincidence in the history of the world" if these outages aren't connected, according to NBC News.

What to watch: Outages are about to become the new normal as organizations race to patch critical vulnerabilities discovered by AI before hackers can use AI to weaponize them.

Go deeper: Why the internet suddenly broke all at once

item.title: Republicans lose hope in Reconciliation 3.0
item.description:
The Senate GOP's last-ditch effort to pass a defense-heavy, $350 billion reconciliation package is dead on arrival without accompanying spending cuts, House Republicans tell Axios.

Why it matters: House Republicans have just 16 days left in session before Democrats take control in January. Many don't want to spend their final days in power adding to the national debt.

  • "My concern is we squander these very few days we have left on something that won't get out of the House," outgoing House Budget Chair Jodey Arrington (R-Texas) told Axios of the Senate's emerging plan.
  • Republicans have already passed two party-line reconciliation bills this Congress: The "one big, beautiful bill" in the summer of 2025, and nearly $70 billion for immigration enforcement in the summer of 2026.

Zoom in: Finding spending offsets could reopen some of the most contentious fights from the GOP's first reconciliation package.

  • Arrington told Axios that Senate Republicans worry that finding cost savings in health care spending could open the door to amendment votes that undo Medicaid cuts in the One Big, Beautiful Bill Act.
  • But Arrington, who didn't run for reelection in 2026, told Axios he doesn't believe the Senate's proposal has the votes to pass the House without offsets.

State of play: Arrington said he raised his concerns with Senate Budget Chair Ron Johnson (R-Wis.), and argued Republicans shouldn't let the risks deter them from pursuing additional spending cuts.

  • "Some Republican members of the Senate might go rogue and might decide to, I don't know, repeal some of the reforms that we put in the 'big, beautiful bill.' Maybe they do it out of spite for President Trump," he said.
  • "The midterms have passed us. We lost, but we still have this window to do what we think is right," he said.

Between the lines: Senate Republicans haven't committed to moving forward with another reconciliation package.

  • Leaving a Wednesday night meeting on reconciliation, Sen. Johnson told reporters the Senate "probably" won't move forward this week, but a reconciliation bill isn't "off the table."
  • Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-S.D.) told reporters he wants to explore working with Democrats on the funding, but that reconciliation remains an "option" Wednesday night.

What they're saying: "It needs to have offsets," Rep. Andrew Clyde (R-Ga.), a member of the conservative House Freedom Caucus, told Axios.

  • Rep. Eli Crane (R-Ariz.), another HFC member, also expressed skepticism about the proposal and its chances of passage. "It's not that I don't want to fund the Department of Defense, but it's always, 'Hey, are we just going to add this to the debt, add this to the deficit,'" he told Axios.

The intrigue: Even if the two chambers can strike a deal, House GOP leaders are struggling to get their own members to show up for votes.

  • GOP leaders were forced to pull a procedural rule vote Wednesday after 14 Republicans failed to show up, leaving leadership without the votes needed to move forward.
  • Rep. Dan Meuser (R-Pa.) told Axios his colleagues need to return to Washington: "I mean, they're getting paid until Jan. 3."

What's next: The House departs Thursday for Thanksgiving recess.

item.title: "There'll be no hostage-taking": The anti-Jeffries rebellion that failed to materialize
item.description:
The left's campaign to whip up a groundswell of opposition to House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) among his members failed in stunning fashion on Wednesday.

Why it matters: Fewer than a dozen members voted against Jeffries' nomination for speaker. That bodes well for Jeffries' ability to manage the House going forward, his allies say.

  • "There'll be no hostage taking," Rep. Troy Carter (D-La.) told Axios.

Driving the news: Jeffries won a resounding victory Wednesday morning when House Democrats met behind closed doors to vote on their nominee for speaker of the House.

  • Out of 264 Democratic House members and non-voting delegates, 251 voted to nominate him, 11 voted against and two did not vote.
  • It was exactly the victory Jeffries' allies had hoped for after Tuesday's announcement that he planned to request a tallied vote rather than being nominated by acclamation.

Reps.-elect Darializa Avila Chevalier (D-N.Y.), Adam Hamawy (D-N.J.), Melat Kiros (D-Colo.), Donavan McKinney (D-Mich.), Chris Rabb (D-Pa.) and Claire Valdez (D-N.Y.) put out a statement shortly after the vote confirming they voted against Jeffries.

  • Rep.-elect Frederick Haynes III (D-Texas) also signed on to that statement, but a spokesperson said in a follow-up statement he "narrowly missed the vote" and that his "intended vote was no."
  • Two other members-elect, Don Leonard (D-Ohio) and Angela Gonzales-Torres (D-Calif.), told Axios they also voted no.
  • Rep.-elect Richard Ojeda (D-N.C.) missed the vote because he was in his district with family following the death of his father, but would have voted for Jeffries, a spokesperson told Axios.

Zoom out: Many of the progressives who ultimately voted for Jeffries did so despite a torrent of phone calls and emails from constituents and grassroots activists urging them not to support him.

  • Numerous high-profile progressives had said before the meeting they would vote for Jeffries, including Reps. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-N.Y.), Pramila Jayapal (D-Wash.) and Greg Casar (D-Texas).
  • Rep. Ayanna Pressley (D-Mass.), who was floated as a potential challenger to Jeffries, told the Boston Globe she voted for him.
  • Rep. Ilhan Omar (D-Minn.) also voted for him, a spokesperson told Axios.

What they're saying: Jayapal said after the vote that Jeffries had "a very strong meeting" with the Congressional Progressive Caucus on Tuesday.

  • "A lot of the issues that matter to us ... on Medicare for All, on immigration, I felt very, very good both about the public direction he's moved in and his commitments to us," she said.
  • "I voted for him, as I have said I was going to do, and I feel like we've been clear about how we're going to continue to need to push."

The intrigue: Three "no" votes were still unaccounted for as of Wednesday night. Several progressives who were seen as potential defectors declined to say how they voted.

  • Rep. Summer Lee (D-Pa.), when asked how she voted, told Axios: "I'll say it to Hakeem, who I will talk to first before I talk to anybody in the press."
  • Spokespeople for Reps. Rashida Tlaib (D-Mich.) and Delia Ramirez (D-Ill.) did not respond to requests for comment.

Between the lines: This isn't the posture of a left flank emboldened to take the fight to party leadership next year, as moderates and Jeffries allies gleefully pointed out.

  • "This has been a manufactured crisis," said Rep. Adam Gray (D-Calif.), a leader of the centrist Blue Dog Coalition.
  • "A handful of folks wanted to amplify their voices and perspectives, and it's always been a handful. It was a handful today."

What's next: The vote now goes to the House floor, where Jeffries needs 218 votes to secure the gavel when the 120th House convenes for the first time on Jan. 3.

  • He can lose more than 30 votes from his current total — which is unlikely — and still come out on top.
  • "They're not going to hold ... Hakeem hostage. It's gone. Move on from that," centrist Rep. Henry Cuellar (D-Texas) told Axios.

item.title: Anthropic valued at over $1 trillion in historic IPO
item.description:
Anthropic on Wednesday raised over $81 billion in a long-awaited IPO that valued the Claude maker at over $1 trillion.

Why it matters: Wall Street expects the AI boom to continue, despite some recent tumult.

Zoom in: Anthropic priced at $83 per share, well above its planned range of $70 to $78 per share.

  • It imputes an initial market cap of $1.08 trillion and a fully diluted value of around $1.5 trillion.
  • Anthropic originally planned to sell 825 million shares, but increased it to 980 million shares.
  • The company also could raise significantly more money if underwriters exercise their so-called "greenshoe" option, while Anthropic also will receive $26 billion via a concurrent private placement from tech giants like Nvidia, Google and Microsoft.
  • Allocation decisions are expected to last several hours on Thursday evening.

Context: Anthropic was valued at $965 billion in its most recent private round. The apples-to-apples comparison would be with the fully diluted value.

  • SpaceX is the current IPO record-holder having raised $86.25 billion, although that included the greenshoe.

What we're watching: Shares are expected to begin trading Thursday, Nov. 19, on the Nasdaq under the ticker "ANT."

item.title: Mississippi senator-elect turns historic win into nationwide Nike offer
item.description:
High school students across the U.S. have a new reason to vie for the top spot in their class: a custom pair of Nike Air Force 1 sneakers, thanks to a request from Mississippi Sen.-elect Scott Colom.

Why it matters: Colom is putting a fresh spin on academic achievement, turning his historic election into a nationwide incentive for students to hit the books — with a little help from Nike and no taxpayer dollars.

What they're saying: Colom initially asked if Nike would celebrate the historic milestone by giving a custom-made version of his favorite sneakers to every Mississippi valedictorian for the 2026-2027 school year.

  • "It would encourage MS students to hit the books the rest of the year! #justdoit," he wrote on X.
  • Nike then upped the ante, extending the offer to valedictorians nationwide.
  • "The athlete mindset makes things possible, including this idea," Nike said.
  • Colom praised Nike for "stepping up to motivate students across the country in this historic moment," and suggested the design honor Hiram Revels, the first Black member of Congress who represented Mississippi.

Context: There were more than 23,000 public high schools in the U.S. during the 2020-2021 school year and more than 3,600 private high schools during the 2019-2020 school year, according to the National Center for Education Statistics.

  • A classic pair of Nike Air Force 1s retails for about $115 on Nike's website.

Zoom in: In January, Colom will become Mississippi's first Democratic senator in nearly four decades and its first Black senator in almost 150 years.

  • The senator-elect pulled off a stunning upset of Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith in the ruby-red state, which hadn't elected a Black senator since Reconstruction.
  • His victory was fueled in part by voters in the Mississippi Delta, where Emmett Till was abducted, Fannie Lou Hamer fought for the ballot and the blues became an American art form.

What we're watching: What Nike cooks up for the nation's brightest students.

item.title: Islam will overtake Christianity as world's largest religion by 2035: Pew
item.description:
Data: Pew Research; Chart: Erin Davis/Axios

Islam is expected to surpass Christianity as the world's largest religion by 2035, according to Pew Research Center projections released Wednesday.

Why it matters: The shift has less to do with people converting to Islam and more to do with who's having more kiddos, a demographic trend poised to reshape the world's religious makeup as Christianity's center of gravity moves to Africa.

By the numbers: Muslims are projected to gain 1.6 billion people through births exceeding deaths from 2020 to 2070, according to new Pew data released Wednesday.

  • Christians are expected to gain 792 million people through natural population change.
  • From 2020 to 2025, Muslim women had an average fertility rate of 3.1 children, compared with 2.5 for Christian women.
  • For all other women, the average was 1.6.

What they're saying: "These religious figures are driven by demographic change," David Voas, a University College London professor who researches secularization, tells Axios.

  • He says the countries growing the fastest — in North Africa, the Middle East, Near East and South Asia — have a relatively high Muslim population, so naturally Islam would eventually be the most populous religion.

Zoom in: The U.S. is expected to lose more Christians than any other country by 2070, even as Christianity grows globally.

  • The U.S. had the world's largest Christian population in 2020, at 217 million. By 2070, that number is expected to drop to 174 million.
  • Meanwhile, the Democratic Republic of the Congo is expected to have nearly 300 million Christians by 2070, far surpassing the U.S. By then, 54% of the world's Christians are projected to live in sub-Saharan Africa.
  • "The center of gravity of Christianity has been shifting towards the global south," Voas says. "Traditionally, we tended to think of Christianity as being a kind of Western religion … but of course Christianity was taken to Africa and around the world, and Africa is now growing faster than anywhere else."

Between the lines: Both Christianity and Islam are expected to lose more followers than they gain through religious switching, including people leaving religion entirely.

  • But Christianity's losses will be far larger.

Zoom out: Islam becoming the world's largest religion doesn't necessarily mean a dramatic shift in global political or cultural power, Voas says.

  • "I would not see any major change in the balance of either political or cultural power, at least in the medium term," he said, adding that it's possible some will assimilate to the local culture and expectations.
  • "There's some wild talk about Europe being taken over by Muslims and so on. That is not going to happen in any foreseeable future."

The bottom line: Islam may soon claim the top spot, but the numbers don't necessarily translate into a seismic shift in global influence.

Go deeper: Tensions erupt in Congress over Republicans' anti-Muslim posts

item.title: Trust, but prepare: How to make sense of AI's age of upheaval
item.description:
Most Americans are baffled and alarmed by the daily, if not hourly, explosion of technical glitches hitting air travel, banks and work products like Microsoft Outlook. The outages seem genuinely scary and related.

  • So what the hell is going on?

The most likely answer: This is the first true wave of unintended consequences of increasingly powerful artificial intelligence hitting us at once.

The big picture: In short, AI is exceptionally good at building software, and therefore exceptionally good at spotting and exploiting bugs in large technical, software-based systems.

  • The glitches come from a mix of sources — some innocuous, some scary, including: routine updates to aging infrastructure; humans scrambling to patch vulnerabilities discovered by AI; hackers exploiting existing weaknesses; and bad actors using swarms of AI agents to launch increasingly sophisticated cyberattacks.

That's the new reality that government officials and AI experts believe we're entering.

  • They expect this period of disruption and heightened vulnerability to persist for months, as powerful new AI tools expose weaknesses buried in decades-old systems.
  • The catchphrase gaining currency: "Software Beirut" — a period of cascading failures, many of our own making, that could grow worse before things get better.

What this means for YOU: Understand the different causes, detailed below, and resist the temptation to panic every time something goes haywire.

  • It's easy to hop on social media and let the algorithm drag you into doomsday thinking.

You should also prepare: Reset and protect your passwords. Keep more cash on hand if possible, in case your bank is down for a day or two. Buy some basic emergency supplies in case power or water do go out. 

  • Sadly, we believe this season of glitches and possible cyberattacks will persist. Better to be prepared.

Here's a more detailed look at the different causes of these glitches or breakdowns:

1. Updates to old systems: The government says last Friday's nationwide airspace outage was simply a case of replacing old copper wires with new fiber that went very, very badly.

  • Aging infrastructure can struggle to accommodate new components. In this case, a network problem overwhelmed legacy equipment, triggering a cascade that grounded flights across the country.

2. AI spotting bugs and humans rushing to fix them: This is one of cyber expert Nicole Perlroth's core scenarios, which went viral this week. AI can find vulnerabilities faster than humans can investigate and patch them. In the frantic sprint to fix those weaknesses before hackers exploit them, systems can break.

  • According to the Washington Sun, banking executives and NSA officials have told lawmakers that rushed efforts to patch AI-discovered vulnerabilities contributed to some of this week's outages.

3. Bad actors attacking vulnerable systems: Across Europe, supermarket refrigerators are being hacked, spoiling millions of dollars' worth of food.

  • No one had "protect the fridges" on their security to-do list this year. But the attacks show how hackers can exploit even the most mundane internet-connected systems — with devastating real-world consequences.

4. AI enabling new forms of cyberattacks: Google said this week it had identified, for the first time, bad actors using AI to find weaknesses and launch cyberattacks entirely on their own — with no human in the loop.

  • If it wasn't already clear, Google warned that "the adversarial AI landscape has reached a critical inflection point."

The bottom line: Most companies and much of government are woefully unprepared for the new era of AI-powered cyberattacks.

  • Their systems are old, clunky and riddled with vulnerabilities. Fortifying them will take enormous amounts of money, time and persistence.
  • The good news: We can see the danger coming, and still have (a little) time to protect ourselves for what may come next.

Axios' Ben Berkowitz and Zachary Basu contributed.

Most Americans are baffled and alarmed by the daily, if not hourly, explosion of technical glitches hitting air travel, banks and work products like Microsoft Outlook. The outages seem genuinely scary and related.

  • So what the hell is going on?

The most likely answer: This is the first true wave of unintended consequences of increasingly powerful artificial intelligence hitting us at once.

The big picture: In short, AI is exceptionally good at building software, and therefore exceptionally good at spotting and exploiting bugs in large technical, software-based systems.

  • The glitches come from a mix of sources — some innocuous, some scary, including: routine updates to aging infrastructure; humans scrambling to patch vulnerabilities discovered by AI; hackers exploiting existing weaknesses; and bad actors using swarms of AI agents to launch increasingly sophisticated cyberattacks.

That's the new reality that government officials and AI experts believe we're entering.

  • They expect this period of disruption and heightened vulnerability to persist for months, as powerful new AI tools expose weaknesses buried in decades-old systems.
  • The catchphrase gaining currency: "Software Beirut" — a period of cascading failures, many of our own making, that could grow worse before things get better.

What this means for YOU: Understand the different causes, detailed below, and resist the temptation to panic every time something goes haywire.

  • It's easy to hop on social media and let the algorithm drag you into doomsday thinking.

You should also prepare: Reset and protect your passwords. Keep more cash on hand if possible, in case your bank is down for a day or two. Buy some basic emergency supplies in case power or water do go out. 

  • Sadly, we believe this season of glitches and possible cyberattacks will persist. Better to be prepared.

Here's a more detailed look at the different causes of these glitches or breakdowns:

1. Updates to old systems: The government says last Friday's nationwide airspace outage was simply a case of replacing old copper wires with new fiber that went very, very badly.

  • Aging infrastructure can struggle to accommodate new components. In this case, a network problem overwhelmed legacy equipment, triggering a cascade that grounded flights across the country.

2. AI spotting bugs and humans rushing to fix them: This is one of cyber expert Nicole Perlroth's core scenarios, which went viral this week. AI can find vulnerabilities faster than humans can investigate and patch them. In the frantic sprint to fix those weaknesses before hackers exploit them, systems can break.

  • According to the Washington Sun, banking executives and NSA officials have told lawmakers that rushed efforts to patch AI-discovered vulnerabilities contributed to some of this week's outages.

3. Bad actors attacking vulnerable systems: Across Europe, supermarket refrigerators are being hacked, spoiling millions of dollars' worth of food.

  • No one had "protect the fridges" on their security to-do list this year. But the attacks show how hackers can exploit even the most mundane internet-connected systems — with devastating real-world consequences.

4. AI enabling new forms of cyberattacks: Google said this week it had identified, for the first time, bad actors using AI to find weaknesses and launch cyberattacks entirely on their own — with no human in the loop.

  • If it wasn't already clear, Google warned that "the adversarial AI landscape has reached a critical inflection point."

The bottom line: Most companies and much of government are woefully unprepared for the new era of AI-powered cyberattacks.

  • Their systems are old, clunky and riddled with vulnerabilities. Fortifying them will take enormous amounts of money, time and persistence.
  • The good news: We can see the danger coming, and still have (a little) time to protect ourselves for what may come next.

Axios' Ben Berkowitz and Zachary Basu contributed.

item.title: The senators who could join Van Hollen's insurgency against Schumer
item.description:
Sen. Chris Van Hollen is picking up endorsements in his challenge to Chuck Schumer for Senate Democratic leader.

Why it matters: The leadership fight exposes divisions within the Democratic Party days after its sweeping midterm victory, with some demanding a new direction and others crediting Schumer for the historic blue wave.

Driving the news: Van Hollen (D-Md.), a senator since 2017, announced Thursday he's challenging Schumer because "we need new leadership."

  • "This is not about any one person — it's about answering the call of the American people."

The other side: Schumer has far more public endorsements than Van Hollen.

  • "Why would you fire the manager when you just won the World Series?" Sen. Angus King (I-Maine) said in a statement of support for Schumer.
  • Van Hollen has disputed Schumer's claim to credit for the party's midterm performance, arguing that the wave was powered by voters rather than leaders in Washington.

By the numbers: Schumer has public support from 14 senators, including himself, compared with five for Van Hollen. A candidate will need 28 or 29 votes to win, depending on the outcome of Alaska's Senate race, where votes are still being counted.

Senators backing Van Hollen

State of play: Van Hollen told MS NOW he has "more than 10" senators on his side, though only four have publicly endorsed him.

  • Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) endorsed Van Hollen on Thursday night, saying he will fight for working families.
  • Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed (D-Mich.) threw his support behind Van Hollen when he announced his challenge Thursday.
  • Sen. Jeff Merkley (D-Ore.) issued an endorsement for Van Hollen Friday afternoon.
  • Incoming Sen. Peggy Flanagan (D-Minn.) endorsed Van Hollen Friday morning after previously calling for new leadership.

Who wants new leadership?

Some sitting senators have called for a leadership change without endorsing Van Hollen.

  • Sen. Elissa Slotkin (D-Mich.) has called for change but hasn't endorsed either candidate.
  • Before Van Hollen announced his candidacy, Sen. Peter Welch (D-Vt.) told NBC 5 Democrats "absolutely are committed to change," but didn't rule out supporting Schumer.

Several Democratic senators-elect have also called for new leadership:

  • Sen.-elect Adam Hamilton (D-Kan.).
  • Sen.-elect Juliana Stratton (D-Ill.).
  • Sen.-elect Troy Jackson (D-Maine).
  • Sen.-elect Annie Andrews (D-S.C.).
  • Sen.-elect Chris Pappas (D-N.H.).

Context: Progressive critics say Schumer hasn't fought hard enough against President Trump and his agenda.

  • Schumer's decision to help advance a Republican-backed government funding bill in March 2025 fueled the progressive backlash against his leadership.
  • The progressive Working Families Party urged Schumer "not to seek another term as Senate Democratic Leader" in a letter, as first reported by Axios. Another labor group has also opposed Schumer and endorsed Van Hollen.

Who's backing Schumer?

Schumer entered the leadership fight with broad support among Senate Democrats.

  • "I have the votes to continue serving as Democratic leader," Schumer (D-N.Y.) said in a statement this week.

Schumer's public supporters include Sen.-elect Sherrod Brown (D-Ohio), Sens. Kirsten Gillibrand (D-N.Y.), John Fetterman (D-Pa.) and King, along with Schumer himself.

  • Also backing Schumer: Sens. Sheldon Whitehouse (R.I.), Ruben Gallego (Ariz.), Mark Kelly (Ariz.), Richard Blumenthal (Conn.), Brian Schatz (Hawaii), Catherine Cortez Masto (Nev.), Jacky Rosen (Nev.), Tammy Baldwin (Wis.) and Jack Reed (R.I.).
  • Schumer also received pre-election endorsements from Sens. Tim Kaine (D-Va.) and Angela Alsobrooks (D-Md.), though neither has publicly reaffirmed that support since Van Hollen entered the race.

Senators who haven't picked a side

Several sitting senators have yet to publicly back either candidate.

  • Sen. Jon Ossoff (D-Ga.), Sen. Chris Murphy (D-Conn.), Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.), Sen. Mark Warner (D-Va.) and Sen. Patty Murray (D-Wash.) have not publicly committed to either candidate.
  • Sen. Andy Kim (D-N.J.) and Sen. Chris Coons (D-Del.) have called for a caucus debate over leadership.
  • Sens. Cory Booker (D-N.J.), Maria Cantwell (D-Wash.) and Raphael Warnock (D-Ga.) have expressed openness to a leadership change without endorsing either candidate.
  • Sen.-elect James Talarico (D-Texas) hasn't committed to Schumer and wants to hear his vision for the Senate.

The 2028 factor

Several potential 2028 presidential contenders face a choice over who should lead Senate Democrats.

  • Ossoff and Booker, both possible 2028 presidential contenders, have yet to pick sides — leaving them to choose between the party's longtime leader and a changing of the guard.
  • Meanwhile, Gallego and Kelly, also seen as possible 2028 contenders, have backed Schumer.

Zoom out: Schumer himself is up for reelection in 2028 and could face a primary challenge from Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-N.Y.), who has also been mentioned as a potential presidential contender.

  • Schumer could also retire rather than seek reelection.

What's next: Senate Democrats will hold a secret-ballot leadership election Dec. 1.

  • Incoming senators will participate, and members can cast their ballots differently from their public endorsements.

item.title: Trump to meet Putin in China amid renewed push to end Ukraine war
item.description:
President Trump will hold a one-on-one meeting with Russian President Vladimir Putin on Thursday during the trilateral summit in China, a U.S. official said.

Why it matters: The meeting in Shenzhen will take place as Trump is making another push for a breakthrough on ending the war in Ukraine.

Driving the news: Also on Thursday, Trump envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner will meet in Berlin with Ukrainian and European officials to work on security guarantees for Ukraine as well as a postwar Europe-Russia security architecture.

  • They want to coordinate ahead of the next round of negotiations with Russia in Abu Dhabi planned for next week.

The big picture: The Trump-Putin meeting, which had not been added to the president schedule until now, will take place on the sidelines of the trilateral summit with Chinese President Xi Jinping.

  • The summit wasn't intended to deal with Ukraine, but U.S. allies are bracing for Trump to make unexpected public statements that serve the interests of Russia and China.
  • "We know that every time President Trump talks to or sees Putin, it translates into bad news for Ukraine and for Europe. We brace for anything," a European diplomat told Axios.

item.title: House Democrats formally nominate Hakeem Jeffries for speaker
item.description:
House Democrats voted at a closed-door caucus meeting Wednesday morning to nominate Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) as their candidate for speaker.

Why it matters: It's a symbolic but significant step that suggests Jeffries has the votes he needs to be elected the first Black House speaker on Jan. 3.

  • Jeffries won 251 of the 262 votes cast, putting him comfortably above the 218 votes he needs to win on the House floor in January.
  • The vote was tallied at Jeffries' request. His allied had initially hoped he would be elected by acclamation, but the Democratic leader changed tack at the 11th hour and decided to call his detractors' bluff.

Between the lines: Wednesday's caucus vote was a secret ballot. On Jan. 3, each House member will have to stand up during a televised proceeding and announce who they are voting for.

  • That could be difficult for the members — particularly progressives — who have been flooded with calls and emails from constituents urging them not to vote for him.
  • Only a handful of incoming House members, including Reps.-elect Angela Gonzales-Torres (D-Calif.) and Don Leonard (D-Ohio), have outright said they will oppose Jeffries thus far.

item.title: U.S. drivers are just absorbing high gasoline prices
item.description:
Pain at the pump may have changed some votes, but it's apparently not prompting big changes in how much Americans drive.

Why it matters: Most driving isn't especially optional, so people are absorbing the cost.

  • This year Americans have paid an additional $88 billion for gasoline relative to a no-war baseline, according to Brown University's Climate Solutions Lab.
  • The Energy Policy Research Foundation finds that U.S. households paid between $300 and $730 more on gasoline in March-August compared to the prior year.

State of play: Gasoline demand from the beginning of March, right after the Iran war started, through early November is very similar to the same stretch last year, per federal data.

  • There's "no discernible evidence of a decline in gasoline consumption," UC-Berkeley energy economist Lucas Davis writes in a new post on the topic.
  • That's despite gasoline prices being 31% higher since the war began compared to the same period last year.

The intrigue: Davis points out that the stubborn demand comes despite polling that shows Americans say high prices are changing their habits.

  • He flags an April Washington Post-ABC News survey that showed 44% of respondents saying they had cut back on driving.
  • Multiple polls show some version of this. For instance, 57% of respondents in a June Gallup survey said high prices were causing them to drive less.

How it works: Davis' post and the chart above rely on the federal Energy Information Administration's measure of gasoline product supplied.

  • EIA calls it a proxy for demand, and measures gasoline leaving the supply chain, including refineries and bulk terminals.
  • There's no perfect measurement. The Transportation Department tracks miles traveled, though there's a lag. The most recent data, for August, does not show a drop-off this year.

The bottom line: "[T]his is a valuable reminder of the gap between what people say and what they do," Davis writes.

  • "Drivers may talk about cutting back, but studies in the economics literature consistently find that gasoline demand is inelastic in the short run," he writes.

item.title: Jeffries nears historic speakership as power shifts in Congress
item.description:
Hakeem Jeffries could soon become America's first Black House speaker, even as Black lawmakers confront rising threats to their power in D.C.

Why it matters: Proposed committee term limits and another round of redistricting could weaken Black lawmakers' influence they spent decades building.

By the numbers: The number of Black lawmakers in the 120th Congress will be stable from the 119th, based on results so far.

  • The House will likely seat 59 Black voting members, down from 61, according to the Joint Center for Political and Economic Studies. All four Black House Republicans are departing, while Black Democrats have gained two seats.
  • Black membership in the U.S. Senate will rise from five to a record seven, including Sens.-elect Scott Colom of Mississippi and Juliana Stratton of Illinois.

Zoom in: Democrats are in the middle of a sometimes messy generational power transfer, with younger lawmakers challenging more senior members for committee chairmanships. Those chairmanships have long helped Congressional Black Caucus members exercise power beyond their numbers.

  • "For CBC members, the power is seniority," Rep. Gregory Meeks (D-N.Y.) told Politico in 2014.
  • "I've been around a while. ... Some wisdom, at least, is important to what we're going through right now," Rep. Bonnie Watson Coleman, 81, (D-N.J.) told Axios in 2025.

Sticking point: Democrats are considering a four-term limit for committee leaders, starting after the 2028 elections, that could eventually force three veteran Black Democrats to step aside as committee leaders.

  • Bennie Thompson, 78, of Mississippi, leads Democrats on Homeland Security.
  • Bobby Scott, 79, of Virginia, leads Democrats on Education and Workforce. He faces a challenge from Connecticut Rep. Jahana Hayes, 53.
  • Maxine Waters, 88, of California, leads Democrats on Financial Services. She faces a challenge from Illinois Rep. Sean Casten, 54.

Zoom out: A Democratic wave helped Black incumbents survive redistricting this year, but that level of support may not be repeated in future elections.

  • The Supreme Court's April ruling in Louisiana v. Callais narrowed protections against maps that watered down the Voting Rights Act, potentially exposing more Black-held districts to redistricting.
  • Texas' new maps pushed veteran Democrat Al Green into a primary against another Black incumbent. Green lost. His heavily redrawn former district elected Latina Democrat Leticia Gutierrez.
  • Black Democrats Shomari Figures of Alabama and Don Davis of North Carolina won in redrawn districts. Louisiana's 6th District heads to a December runoff.

Between the lines: Hispanic Democrats are also gaining influence, with their numbers in Congress reaching new highs.

  • California Rep. Pete Aguilar, a Hispanic Democrat, appears headed for majority whip, a top party leadership job.
  • The Congressional Hispanic Caucus expects 55 members, including senators and Puerto Rico's nonvoting resident commissioner — its largest membership since its 1976 founding.

Yes, but: Hispanic gains don't necessarily come at Black lawmakers' expense.

  • Hispanic Democrats on Financial Services have backed Waters, showing how the two groups can work together as their members seek more influence.
  • Younger lawmakers say term limits could open doors for the next generation of Black and Hispanic leaders.

item.title: Xi Jinping breaks protocol to greet and hug Trump at China airport
item.description:
Chinese President Xi Jinping greeted President Trump in a surprise appearance on the tarmac in Shenzhen, China, on Wednesday.

Why it matters: Xi paid Trump a special honor by greeting him on the tarmac, reciprocating a gesture by Trump during Xi's state visit to Washington in September.

  • The two are expected to hold a summit Thursday with Russian President Vladimir Putin, where the three are expected to talk about nuclear arms control, Iran, Ukraine, trade and AI chips.

Driving the news: Trump arrived in China for the annual APEC conference just hours after spending time in the Philippines.

  • Xi met Trump at the bottom of Air Force One's stairs. The two leaders shook hands, then embraced.
  • Dozens of performers, waving pom-poms, stood on a red carpet outside the plane, chanting and cheering for Trump's arrival.

Context: Xi's surprise appearance was an unusual diplomatic gesture, per multiple reports. The Chinese president did not personally greet Trump when he visited Beijing in May.

  • Similarly, when Putin visited Shenzhen earlier today, he was greeted by Xi's chief of staff Cai Qi.
  • Xi met former President Obama at the airport in 2009 when Xi was still vice president.

Flashback: In September 2025, Trump welcomed President Xi at Joint Base Andrews for the Chinese leader's state visit to Washington, D.C. American presidents typically receive foreign leaders at the White House.

  • Trump met Xi at the bottom of the stairs after Xi's jet landed at the U.S. military base.

Go deeper: U.S. allies on edge as Trump heads to summit with Xi and Putin

Context: Xi's surprise appearance was an unusual diplomatic gesture, per multiple reports. The Chinese president did not personally greet Trump when he visited Beijing in May.

  • Similarly, when Putin visited Shenzhen earlier today, he was greeted by Xi's chief of staff Cai Qi.
  • Xi met former President Obama at the airport in 2009 when Xi was still vice president.

Flashback: In September 2025, Trump welcomed President Xi at Joint Base Andrews for the Chinese leader's state visit to Washington, D.C. American presidents typically receive foreign leaders at the White House.

  • Trump met Xi at the bottom of the stairs after Xi's jet landed at the U.S. military base.

Go deeper: U.S. allies on edge as Trump heads to summit with Xi and Putin

item.title: House Dems prepare for broad Trump family probe
item.description:
Rep. Robert Garcia (D-Calif.), incoming chair of the House Oversight Committee, is laying the groundwork for a wave of investigations into President Trump's inner circle.

Why it matters: It's going to be a long two years in Washington, as Democrats emboldened by the blue wave step up their scrutiny of those closest to the president and the administration.

Driving the news: Garcia is sending document-retention letters Wednesday to Vice President Vance, Don Jr., Eric Trump, Jared Kushner, Kimberly Guilfoyle, Stephen Miller, Susie Wiles, Kristi Noem, Corey Lewandowski, Attorney General Todd Blanche and more.

  • "This is just the beginning," Garcia said in a statement.

What to watch: How the administration responds.

  • Already, at least one U.S. Attorney is going after other Democrats who've promised oversight actions in the coming Congress.

This is a developing story.
