item.title: America's measles return leaves infants vulnerable
item.description:
The loss of the United States' measles elimination status is a particularly worrisome sign for infants in hot spots who are too young to be vaccinated against the disease.

Why it matters: Outbreaks still may be concentrated within certain parts of the country. But infants and other unvaccinated people are living with a continuous threat.

Driving the news: The Pan American Health Organization announced on Tuesday that it revoked the U.S. status after 26 years, as expected.

  • That's after state reports of 7,700 cases and 10 deaths since measles first began spreading in Texas early last year, according to the New York Times. (The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention currently reports only nine deaths.)
  • Hundreds of people — often unvaccinated children — have been hospitalized.

State of play: The measles-mumps-rubella vaccine is highly effective, meaning the vast majority of cases today occur in people who haven't received an immunization against the disease.

  • Just over 1 in 10 of those infected this year were hospitalized, but that jumps to 17% among children under 5 years old, per the CDC.

Between the lines: For most of the population, remaining unvaccinated against measles is a choice, albeit one parents make for their children.

  • But for the youngest Americans, receiving a vaccine isn't an option for several months.
  • The earliest an infant can receive an immunization against measles is at 6 months, with the official recommendation for most children being a first dose between 12 and 15 months.
  • Though infants do receive protective antibodies against measles from their mothers, those gradually decline over their first months of life.

What they're saying: "Most babies don't receive a first measles vaccine until age 1. With measles endemic again, parents can no longer assume grocery stores, airports, churches, or even pediatricians' offices are safe spaces," Jerome Adams, President Trump's first-term surgeon general, posted on X.

  • "The community protection we took for granted is gone, and U.S. moms now must live in fear that their babies will be harmed by a completely preventable disease, while they do [everyday] tasks."
  • Some experts are raising the prospect of an official three-dose schedule for the MMR vaccine, in which all infants get the earlier dose in addition to the two already recommended.

Details: Infants can receive a dose as early as 6 months if they live in or are visiting places with a high risk of exposure or are traveling internationally.

  • "For those under 6 months of age, the best thing we can do is awareness and improve that cocoon and immunity the best that we can," said Elizabeth Murray, a pediatric emergency medicine doctor and a spokesperson for the American Academy of Pediatrics.
  • Parents should "make sure whoever you are around or whoever is around your baby is up to date on all of their vaccines," she added.

Zoom in: New research has also documented how measles infections acquired during pregnancy are becoming more common and can have dire consequences.

  • Between January 2025 and the end of September this year, 112 cases of measles during pregnancy — almost entirely among unvaccinated women — and 13 cases of congenital measles (meaning a case in a newborn contracted from its mother) were reported to the CDC, according to research published this week in the New England Journal of Medicine.
  • Nearly a quarter of the pregnant women were hospitalized for reasons other than labor, and adverse outcomes for babies delivered within 14 days of their mothers developing a measles rash included preterm delivery and admission to intensive care.
  • Congenital measles can also result in severe neurologic complications, the report notes.

The bottom line: "We will likely be dealing with measles this year, next year, and the year after," Paul Offit, director of the Vaccine Education Center at Children's Hospital of Philadelphia, wrote on Substack.

  • "And, until immunization rates increase, we will continue to see more suffering, more hospitalizations, and more deaths from this entirely preventable infection."

item.title: The terrifying rise of AI hacking tools
item.description:
A new breed of widely available AI tools is helping hackers launch cyberattacks around the clock, breaching corporate networks in a matter of hours and overwhelming defenders.

Why it matters: AI-enabled hacking is still in its infancy, but open-source tools — which are free to download — are fundamentally changing the economics of cybercrime.

  • Hackers can launch self-adjusting attack plans, allowing agents to find vulnerabilities and steal credentials, sometimes before human defenders realize their systems are being probed.

Driving the news: Recent cyberattacks involving publicly available "AI agent frameworks" are drawing warnings about how quickly hackers can infiltrate corporate networks.

  • The FBI warned Friday that hackers have used an AI framework called Artex to attack organizations worldwide, with some intrusions progressing from initial targeting to privileged access in less than three hours.
  • In a separate report Friday, Amazon said hackers used Artex to steal AI model credentials, then used those stolen resources to power additional attacks.
  • Last week, developer platform Railway and blockchain infrastructure provider Chainstack also reported attacks involving Artex.
  • Palo Alto Networks said Thursday that Chinese-speaking hackers used another open-source framework, Cairn, to conduct 25 operations against at least 19 organizations between August and September. In a separate report Monday, Google said hackers used Cairn during an intrusion into the U.S. aerospace sector.
  • CrowdStrike also saw one group using Artex to target more than 200 organizations worldwide over 11 days last month.

Reality check: Cyberattacks are still scary, and tech resiliency is still built on a faulty internet foundation, making mishaps possible even without clear evidence of AI-assisted hacks.

  • A litany of popular services — including Microsoft, Apple, Chase, United, Workday, the Federal Aviation Administration and the National Security Agency — have all reported outages in the last week.
  • An unknown group infected about 178 major websites with crypto-stealing malware through the Optimizely Web Experimentation platform in less than a day, according to Report URI. Affected websites included Zoom, the BBC, CNN, Salesforce, GitLab and Ikea, and AI doesn't seem to be involved as of now.

What they're saying: "We're seeing more active attacks than ever right now," Sam Rubin, senior vice president of Palo Alto Networks' Unit 42 threat intelligence and consulting unit, told Axios.

  • "The open-weight models are getting close to frontier-level capabilities," and when combined with tools like Artex and Cairn, they are "really hitting organizations hard," he added.
  • Incident response firms worldwide are stretched to capacity, with some turning away cases because they lack resources, John Hultquist, chief analyst at Google's threat intelligence group, told Axios.

How it works: Artex and Cairn use AI agents to automate tasks hackers traditionally performed themselves.

  • A hacker gives the framework a target and an objective, such as breaking into a company's network.
  • AI agents develop attack plans, search for vulnerabilities and use hacking tools to test possible entry points.
  • The agents share findings and adjust tactics when something fails, allowing them to operate around the clock without constant human supervision.

Between the lines: Hackers are also stealing the computing resources needed to sustain their AI-powered attacks.

  • Amazon's findings show how attackers can steal access to AI models and use that access to find more credentials, expanding their operations without paying for the computing power.

The intrigue: These frameworks aren't necessarily good at hiding their activity, but that might not matter.

  • Hultquist said autonomous attacks generate substantial suspicious activity, potentially making them easier to detect.
  • But financially motivated hackers may only need to steal valuable information before defenders stop them.
  • He also warned that state-backed hackers could use these capabilities to disrupt critical systems before defenders can intervene.

What we're watching: Security teams may need to fundamentally change their defenses to keep pace with automated attacks.

item.title: Alaska Native strongholds push Peltola into Senate history
item.description:
Mary Peltola's path to Senate history ran through four Alaska Native strongholds that delivered more than half of her statewide first-choice lead.

Why it matters: The Yup'ik Democrat is the nation's first Alaska Native U.S. senator, powered by communities that endured disenfranchisement, forced displacement and federal violence.

  • The win amplifies their voice on tribal sovereignty and subsistence rights after decades of neglect and discrimination — much as Mississippi Delta Black voters powered Democrat Scott Colom to his surprising Senate victory.

By the numbers: Peltola led Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan by roughly 12,400 first-choice votes statewide in Alaska's Nov. 17 unofficial count. Four western and northern House districts delivered a combined margin of about 6,700 votes.

  • In Bristol Bay/Aleutians, for example, Peltola led by roughly 1,150 votes.
  • In Bethel/Yukon-Kuskokwim Delta and Western Alaska/Norton Sound, she led by roughly 2,300 votes.
  • In North Slope/Northwest Arctic, she led by approximately 900 votes.

Stunning stat: Those four districts accounted for just about 5% of Alaska's first-choice Senate votes, but roughly 55% of Peltola's statewide lead.

  • Alaska's 2021 redistricting report identifies Districts 37–40 as Alaska Native-controlled.
  • Alaska Natives, alone or in combination, accounted for 85.8% of the voting-age population in District 38, 85.1% in 39, 62% in 40 and 43.8% in 37, using 2020 census figures.
  • About 22% of Alaska residents identified as American Indian or Alaska Native, alone or in combination with another race, according to the 2020 census.

State of play: Peltola carried the 50% margin needed to avoid Alaska's ranked-choice tabulation, where lower-ranked preferences from other candidates' supporters could have tipped the race toward another candidate.

  • Michelle Sparck of the nonpartisan Get Out the Native Vote effort told KNBA that Native groups mounted aggressive outreach, including in Native languages.
  • Organizers saw gains in some rural communities, though definitive statewide turnout comparisons remain pending.

Zoom in: In Kwethluk, the Yup'ik village where Peltola grew up, she outpolled Sullivan 136–9. In Savoonga on St. Lawrence Island, she led 157–5.

  • In Tlingit communities Angoon and Kake, she led 109–22 and 140–30, respectively.
  • The Navy apologized in 2024 for destroying Angoon in 1882 and bombarding and burning Kake in 1869.

Flashback: In 1915, Alaska's territorial lawmakers required Native citizenship applicants to abandon tribal ties and customs.

  • In 1925, after Congress extended citizenship to Native Americans, Alaska imposed an English literacy requirement that disenfranchised many Native voters.
  • During World War II, the U.S. removed 881 Unangax̂ people from nine villages to Southeast Alaska camps plagued by disease and poor shelter.

The intrigue: In April 1969, Sen. Ted Kennedy traveled 3,600 miles over three days through Native communities, following a poverty tour his slain brother Robert had planned.

  • TIME documented villages with 60% unemployment and homes without plumbing, comparing the trip to Robert's visits to Appalachia and the Mississippi Delta.
  • Partisan accusations over publicity overshadowed the poverty Kennedy sought to expose.

Yes, but: Alaska Native voters today don't vote as a bloc. The Alaska Federation of Natives endorsed no one in the Senate race. And district returns can't establish how individual Native voters voted — or prove a statewide turnout surge.

Between the lines: In communities covered by the EPA's Alaska Native Villages data, 1,129 homes lacked drinking water, wastewater service or both in 2025, down from 6,892 in 2005, per an EPA report.

  • Native leaders continue pressing Washington on subsistence rights, infrastructure, education and self-determination.

item.title: Mary Peltola unseats Republican Dan Sullivan in Alaska, extending Democratic wave
item.description:
Former Democratic Rep. Mary Peltola has defeated two-term Republican Sen. Dan S. Sullivan, flipping another GOP-held seat in a state President Trump carried comfortably in 2024, the AP projects.

Why it matters: Peltola becomes the first Democrat elected to the Senate from Alaska since 2008, extending a historic blue wave in a race marred by controversy.

  • Her victory comes in a state Trump carried by 13 points in 2024, underscoring the extraordinary reach of the Democratic backlash against his second term.
  • It also delivers another blow to Republicans after sweeping Democratic victories in states including Texas, Ohio, Iowa and South Carolina.

What they're saying: "As a lifelong Alaskan who has dedicated my career to serving our state, there is no greater honor than having Alaskans' support in our fight to take on corporate greed, lower costs, and put Alaska first," Peltola wrote on X Tuesday evening.

  • "Thank you, Alaska. Let's get to work," she added.

State of play: The race drew scrutiny after The New York Times reported allegations that Democratic operatives recruited another candidate named Dan Sullivan to draw votes from the incumbent.

  • Peltola's campaign denied involvement, but the reporting prompted Alaska's Republican governor, Mike Dunleavy, to order an investigation into whether state laws were broken.
  • The Justice Department also launched a criminal investigation and subpoenaed people connected to the alleged effort. No one involved in the race has been charged with a crime.

On the campaign trail, the candidates clashed over the cost of living, the Iran war and Alaska's energy industry, with Peltola challenging Sullivan's record in Washington.

  • Peltola campaigned on her signature "fish, family and freedom" message, emphasizing affordability, protecting Alaska's fisheries and putting the state's interests ahead of party politics.
  • Trump traveled to Alaska in October to rally support for Sullivan, whom he praised as one of Washington's most respected senators.
  • Sullivan embraced the president's support, betting it would energize Republican voters despite their party's political headwinds.

The big picture: Alaska has long leaned Republican, but Peltola's ability to win crossover support — including votes from Republicans who ranked her above former Gov. Sarah Palin in 2022 — helped put the state in play for Democrats.

  • Peltola made history in that 2022 special election as the first Alaska Native elected to Congress. She won a full term later that year before losing her House seat to Republican Nick Begich in 2024.
  • Sullivan, a former Alaska attorney general and Marine Corps veteran, has represented Alaska in the Senate since 2015. The two-term Republican campaigned on his record on energy development and national security.

Context: Another candidate named Dan Sullivan — a retired teacher from Petersburg, Alaska, listed on the ballot as Daniel J. Sullivan Jr. — became a factor in the race.

  • The Trump administration sued Alaska on Oct. 22, seeking to delay certification if Sen. Sullivan lost and votes for the other Dan Sullivan could have changed the outcome.
  • A federal judge dismissed the lawsuit on Nov. 1, ruling that the administration lacked standing to bring the case and that its proposed remedy was unworkable. The Justice Department appealed the decision.
  • Sen. Sullivan committed to accepting the results even if he didn't win.

How it works: Alaska's ranked-choice voting system added another wrinkle.

  • Voters rank candidates in order of preference. If no candidate wins a majority of first-choice votes, the last-place candidate is eliminated and votes for that candidate are redistributed according to voters' next available choices. The process repeats until a candidate wins a majority.

What's next: Alaska election officials will complete the remaining certification steps, with the Justice Department's appeal potentially affecting the process.

item.title: Why the internet suddenly broke all at once
item.description:
Americans were locked out of bank accounts, blocked from boarding flights and unable to check emails in rapid succession over the past week.

Why it matters: The internet immediately pointed fingers toward an AI agent doomsday, sending people into a frenzy that the Big One™was about to happen.

Reality check: Experts tell Axios these disruptions don't appear linked to hacking or a kind of cyber apocalypse.

  • To the extent they involve AI, the incidents may have more to do with widespread efforts to fix outdated code as institutions try to safeguard their systems from a potential hacking onslaught.
  • Downdetector data also show that while the seven days through Monday represent the highest number of weekly outages in the last 12 months, the pattern over longer periods such as 30 days is far from unprecedented.

Driving the news: National security officials and Wall Street executives have told lawmakers the outages stem from efforts to fix software bugs found by AI systems, according to The Washington Sun.

  • Global institutions are in an all-out race to avoid a "bugmageddon," a scenario in which AI-assisted hackers are able to find and exploit vulnerabilities across the internet before they can be fixed.
  • Apparently, that process has created its own instabilities.

Catch up quick: Some Americans struggled to access JPMorgan Chase banking services Monday.

  • United Airlines briefly delayed departing flights later that day, days after the FAA executed the longest nationwide ground stop since 9/11.
  • Microsoft Outlook's outage left users unable to access emails and other Microsoft 365 services.
  • Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin suggested Monday that AI systems capable of writing and changing code could be contributing to the outages.

Yes, but: No evidence so far points to AI-assisted hacking. In most cases, the outages have been attributed to software patching and appear otherwise unrelated, even as small technical problems snowballed into big ones.

  • Chase blamed an internal software bug that delayed transactions involving other banks.
  • United cited a technology problem; the FAA said a flood of network traffic destabilized older, legacy equipment.
  • Microsoft cited a months-old bug, increased traffic and reduced server capacity.

Between the lines: There are ways AI may have played a role that have nothing to do with hacking.

  • Institutions around the world are racing to update software in order to solidify systems, given that AI models are capable of finding and exploiting vulnerabilities with shocking speed.
  • That race has accelerated a lot of coding work, a process that can lead to more downtime, outages and unexpected hiccups, experts say.
  • AI has also dramatically accelerated the rate at which engineers write and improve software, leading to new bottlenecks for reviewing the safety and reliability of new code. To the extent reviewers or the systems they work with are overwhelmed, mistakes are possible.

What they're saying: Increasingly complex systems are being pushed to operate faster and cheaper without enough attention to how they might fail, David Woods, a professor emeritus of integrated systems engineering at Ohio State University, told Axios.

  • "We're cutting out the cross checks, we're cutting out the tests, we're cutting out the stress tests, we're cutting out the safeguards," Woods says.
  • "Humans see patterns in everything, regardless of whether they're there, and generally interpret coincidences as conspiracies," said Bruce Schneier, a security technologist. "It's human psychology."
  • "There's very little that these incidents have in common, actually," Liz Fong-Jones a technical fellow at Honeycomb tells Axios. "No one notices when things go right."

By the numbers: Downdetector received nearly 6 million U.S. problem reports in the seven days ending Nov. 16, the highest weekly total in a year, Ookla analyst Luke Kehoe tells Axios.

  • However, the past 30 days saw just three major outages, compared with a typical five.

The intrigue: Some experts doubt that AI is to blame.

  • "The outages that we've seen are a decades-old phenomenon ... cascading failures," Fong-Jones says. "Nothing to do with writing code, nothing to do with shipping code with AI."

Zoom in: Fong-Jones compares cascading failures to a busy intersection where a traffic light stops working. Cars back up, drivers turn to surrounding streets, and soon the entire area is gridlocked.

  • That's essentially what happened at Microsoft, where a software bug combined with increased traffic and reduced capacity, overwhelming servers as they tried to recover.

The bottom line: New technology can make systems faster and more efficient, but it can't eliminate the unexpected.

  • When companies rush to embrace it without preparing for what could go wrong, "the world bites back and bites your ass," Woods warns.

Editor's note: This story was updated to offer additional detail on potential causes of recent outages.

item.title: House Dems can't stand the speaker vote drama anymore
item.description:
House Democrats aren't unanimous on whether House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) should be speaker, but they pretty much all agree on two things: He probably will be speaker, and they just want this to be over.

Why it matters: Their phones and emails are still being blown up by constituents and grassroots activists urging them to do what they can to block Jeffries from securing the speaker gavel.

  • There isn't much Jeffries' skeptics and detractors on Capitol Hill can do: He is set to easily win his caucus' nomination on Wednesday and then be formally elected to the role on Jan. 3.
  • Rep.-elect Jake Johnson (D-Minn.), who told Axios last week he was undecided, said Tuesday he met with Jeffries and was "assured" votes on his two key issues: Ending the Trump administration's tariffs and the war in Iran.
  • "I'll be voting for Leader Jeffries," Johnson told Axios.

State of play: The movement to deny Jeffries the speakership has proliferated online and among the progressive grassroots but has struggled to gain a foothold on Capitol Hill.

  • A handful of members of the progressive "Bloc" — and some other newly elected members in deeply red district — have voiced skepticism of Jeffries, but only in a few cases has that evolved into outright opposition.
  • "As of now, I'm a 'no,'" Rep.-elect Angela Gonzales-Torres (D-Calif.) told Axios on Wednesday. "The people are saying we deserve better, and better is possible."

Reality check: Nobody is challenging Jeffries. Some people floated as potential potential challengers, such as Rep. Jamie Raskin (D-Md.), have firmly ruled it out.

  • Rep. Ayanna Pressley (D-Mass.), the subject of an online petition urging her to seek the role, has privately told colleagues she is not running but been more equivocal in public.
  • "I'm very humbled to even be in conversation," Pressley said at a town hall on Monday.
  • She added that she was "making no declarations or announcements" at that event and does not "need to be the speaker of the House to speak for the people."

What we're hearing: Some of Pressley's fellow Congressional Progressive Caucus members, granted anonymity to speak candidly, expressed frustration that she hasn't more forcefully tamped down the speculation.

  • "She's only playing coy with people online," one CPC member told Axios. "The rest of us know she's not running. But that's generating additional calls and making people … even more pissed off in the end."
  • Said another CPC member: "Many of us feel like she's stringing people along online to make them think that she's running and it's just not reality. "
  • A third CPC member complained that it's "a bit selfish," with an incoming CPC member saying "it's not real" and chalking it up to Congress being an "attention economy."

Yes, but: A second incoming CPC member said the grassroots would be "blowing us up regardless" of whether Pressley shut down the speculation or not.

  • "It's true that the percentage of emails that mention her has grown, but the number was large to begin with," the member-elect added.

What they're saying: "Everyone's trying to use whatever leverage they have and I think she's probably hoping that maybe this could be a way to make sure her voice is heard," said Rep. Pramila Jayapal (D-Wash.).

  • Gonzales-Torres said she is "fully behind" the policy agenda Pressley has laid out but, asked if she would vote for her for speaker, said, "Where does she stand? What is she doing? Do you know?"
  • Rep.-elect Don Leonard (D-Ohio), one of Jeffries' most outspoken critics in the freshman class, said in a Breaking Points interview that Pressley "would have my support."
  • Rep.-elect Dan Koh (D-Mass.) said Pressley "would be a great speaker but she's not running, so it's a hypothetical."

What's next: House Democrats will meet behind closed-doors Wednesday to vote on their nominee for speaker and other caucus leadership roles.

  • Jeffries plans to request a tallied vote, rather than being nominated by acclamation.
  • He needs a simple majority among Democrats to secure the nomination but at least 218 votes on the House floor to formally win the gavel on Jan. 3. Democrats are expected to have a majority of at least 260 seats, giving Jeffries a wide margin for error.

The bottom line: "The whole thing has been a stupid clusterfuck," one of the CPC members told Axios. "This is such a distraction from reality."

item.title: Scoop: White House drops Heidi Overton's FDA nomination
item.description:
The White House is dropping Heidi Overton's nomination to lead the Food and Drug Administration because of a lack of congressional support, Axios has learned.

Why it matters: The decision means the Trump administration will have to find a new candidate to lead the FDA as HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. looks to advance his Make America Healthy Again agenda.

  • "FDA nominee Heidi Overton lacks the support on the Hill to move forward with her confirmation," a senior administration official told Axios late Tuesday.

Zoom in: Overton, a physician and deputy director of the White House Domestic Policy Council, was nominated by President Trump in August.

  • She had drawn criticism from segments of the MAHA movement that saw her siding with health and agriculture interests and helping undermine Kennedy agenda.
  • Antiabortion forces also questioned her commitment to tightening rules for prescribing the abortion pill mifepristone.

The backstory: Her nomination faced opposition from Democrats and skepticism from some Republican senators, including Sen. Bill Cassidy (R-La.), chair of the Senate's Health, Education, Labor and Pensions (HELP) Committee.

  • Cassidy said he had "strong concerns" about Overton's role in the administration's efforts to change childhood vaccine recommendations, which he called "almost disqualifying."

What they're saying: "We need to go in a new direction at FDA, and everybody fully supports Secretary Kennedy's vision to Make America Healthy Again and get back to a more populist and common-sense approach to health in America," the senior administration official said.

  • The White House had tried to shore up her nomination Monday, posting on social media an account from the former dean of the University of New Mexico School of Medicine supporting Overton's confirmation.

What's next: The HELP committee had been scheduled to vote on Overton's nomination on Wednesday.

  • The FDA has been led by acting Commissioner Kyle Diamantas since Marty Makary resigned in May.

item.title: Exclusive: Donald Trump Jr. signals investors underestimated AI pushback
item.description:
Donald Trump Jr. signaled that investors underestimated the political pushback to the AI ecosystem in an interview at Axios' annual BFD summit in New York.

The big picture: The 2026 midterms reflected deep distrust of the AI race, with voters approving dozens of moratoriums on data centers — which President Trump rallied around.

Driving the news: Trump Jr. asserted that "a lot of" the pushback "is manufactured." But he added "that doesn't mean it's not real" in an interview with Axios Pro Rata author Dan Primack Tuesday.

  • "I think some of the big founders of the biggest [AI] companies out there probably have not done themselves the best service as [a] marketing department," he said, adding that they're "probably not the best messengers when they basically say, 'AI is gonna rule the world, and you should be thrilled about it.'"
  • Asked by Primack if investors, peers or the pair themselves underestimated the populist pushback to AI, Trump Jr. said, "I think we saw that very clearly."
  • He likened AI to other "any great innovation," but said, "This is gonna be one of those things, but it is going to take some time for people to learn how to adapt that into their regular lives."

State of play: Trump Jr. spoke with Primack alongside 1789 Capital co-founder Omeed Malik, whose venture Trump Jr. joined in 2024. The investment firm has since exploded from overseeing a few hundred million dollars to billions.

Zoom in: Trump Jr. agreed that the rage toward data centers represents a broader concern over growing AI influence.

  • That public anger is becoming key to candidates: Democrats in six early 2028 primary states expect their presidential nominee to prioritize AI regulations, according to new polling data first reported by Axios' Maria Curi.
  • Ahead of the midterms, Republicans took note of the sagging views of the data centers needed to power the AI boom. While Trump has prioritized self-regulation for the industry, the November results raise questions about how Republicans will tackle the tech moving forward.

Zoom out: Asked if there was anything Democrats and the White House could agree on after a November shellacking that could be good for business, he said "we've got to focus" on costs and inflation.

  • But he argued that "the second they win ... it's about investigations" — which Trump Jr. could find himself targeted by.

Editor's note: This story was updated with additional context throughout.

item.title: "We will remain thoughtful": Nvidia says it will continue to backstop AI ecosystem
item.description:
Nvidia's interim CEO said Tuesday that the company will be "disciplined" as it decides how much to invest in neoclouds and other AI customers going forward.

Why it matters: Nvidia isn't just the biggest chip partner for AI startups — it's a major source of capital.

What they're saying: "Our momentum is real," interim CEO Colette Kress said at the end of a conference call with investors and analysts. "Our demand is accelerating. Our supply is growing. Our customers and our partners are with us, and employees are committed. We've got this."

  • She said the company would continue to use its balance sheet and support startups and the broader AI ecosystem, but she made clear it won't be a blank check.
  • "As the market matures and additional sources of capital become available, we are rigorously evaluating future investments, commitments, and guarantees," she added.

In particular, Kress said the company would continue to be "disciplined and selective in our support" for so-called neoclouds.

  • Those companies provide additional computing capacity to big AI players as well as smaller and regional operators. "Our neoclouds have been so instrumental in terms of both supporting enterprises and supporting many of the different countries around the world."
  • CoreWeave and Nebius, two such neoclouds, each jumped in after-hours trading.

Zoom in: Kress didn't name-check any other specific customers but said the company would offer capital to suppliers to help them move quickly.

  • Nvidia will provide financing assistance or guarantees to some "very strong customers," she said.
  • The chip-maker will "look very deeply" into whether guarantees are needed and conduct "a lot of work to understand if those are the right types of investments we need to make."

Catch up quick: Former CEO Jensen Huang resigned last week after revelations that he had a relationship with a woman who allegedly had ties to Chinese intelligence.

  • She was also an executive with a major Nvidia customer that allegedly helped Chinese AI companies gain access to cutting-edge Nvidia technology while the U.S. had banned some chip sales to the country.

On the call, Nvidia board chair Harvey Jones threw cold water on the notion of a quick return for Huang. "The Nvidia board unanimously accepted his resignation and does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO," he said.

  • The company said it wouldn't be taking questions on Huang's departure or its ongoing investigation into his actions.

item.title: Nvidia posts strong earnings amid Jensen Huang exit, reported SEC probe
item.description:
Nvidia posted a stronger-than-expected third quarter and a bullish outlook in its first earnings report after Jensen Huang was ousted as CEO in a scandal that has reportedly spawned an SEC investigation.

  • On the company's earnings call, newly appointed chairman Harvey Jones said the board "does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO," despite a movement among some employees and investors to bring him back.

Why it matters: Nvidia remains squarely at the center of the AI economy — and investors are anxious for guidance on the company's strategic roadmap following Huang's sudden exit.

Zoom in: Nvidia recorded quarterly revenue of $115.8 billion and net income of $65.3 billion, both more than doubling its performance from a year earlier.

  • S&P Capital IQ analysts had expected revenue of $108.7 billion and net income of $60.5 billion.
  • The company's data center revenue — its largest segment — rose 110% from a year ago to $107.6 billion.

The showing — which included a whopping gross profit margin of 74.8% — immediately calmed investors who have shaved more than $1 trillion off of Nvidia's market cap since the Huang scandal broke.

  • The stock was up as much as 5% in after-hours trading Tuesday following the company's earnings call.

It marks the first moment for interim CEO Colette Kress — who is also still serving as CFO — to exert her leadership during the most tumultuous moment in the company's history.

  • On the earnings call, she struck a steady tone, saying the company's momentum and innovation remain substantial.
  • "We've got this," she said.
  • Kress didn't mention Huang by name on the call but acknowledged the turbulent time and the "diverse" opinions — an apparent reference to the campaign to bring back Huang.

What we're watching: WSJ reported Tuesday afternoon that the SEC has opened a civil probe into the company.

  • An SEC spokesperson declined to comment.
  • Nvidia reps did not immediately respond to a request for comment, and the executives didn't discuss it on the call — but they said their quarterly 10Q filing with the SEC will be delayed.

The earnings call came hours after Huang posted a public letter saying he'd be "honored" to return as CEO.

  • Tech analyst Dan Ives earlier said the board could face a special shareholder meeting called by at least 15% of shareholders.
  • Jones said the company would not take questions on Huang's exit. He said the board would consider external and internal candidates and wants to move "as quickly as possible" but won't make a move until it finds "exactly the right person."

The intrigue: Huang reportedly faced pushback from Kress as he pushed financing deals to backstop the AI ecosystem.

  • On Tuesday's call, Kress signaled that the company would continue to provide financing where appropriate but would be "selective" and ensure that guarantees are necessary.

Editor's note: This story was updated to include comments from Nvidia chairman Harvey Jones and interim CEO Colette Kress made on the company's earnings call.

Nvidia posted a stronger-than-expected third quarter and a bullish outlook in its first earnings report after Jensen Huang was ousted as CEO in a scandal that has reportedly spawned an SEC investigation.

  • On the company's earnings call, newly appointed chairman Harvey Jones said the board "does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO," despite a movement among some employees and investors to bring him back.

Why it matters: Nvidia remains squarely at the center of the AI economy — and investors are anxious for guidance on the company's strategic roadmap following Huang's sudden exit.

Zoom in: Nvidia recorded quarterly revenue of $115.8 billion and net income of $65.3 billion, both more than doubling its performance from a year earlier.

  • S&P Capital IQ analysts had expected revenue of $108.7 billion and net income of $60.5 billion.
  • The company's data center revenue — its largest segment — rose 110% from a year ago to $107.6 billion.

The showing — which included a whopping gross profit margin of 74.8% — immediately calmed investors who have shaved more than $1 trillion off of Nvidia's market cap since the Huang scandal broke.

  • The stock was up as much as 5% in after-hours trading Tuesday following the company's earnings call.

It marks the first moment for interim CEO Colette Kress — who is also still serving as CFO — to exert her leadership during the most tumultuous moment in the company's history.

  • On the earnings call, she struck a steady tone, saying the company's momentum and innovation remain substantial.
  • "We've got this," she said.

item.title: Duffy's $50 billion request gets chilly reception from Senate GOP
item.description:
Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy's $50 billion request to overhaul the nation's air traffic control system is getting a chilly reception from Senate Republicans, who are balking at the hefty price tag.

Why it matters: The pushback from within President Trump's own party casts doubt on the administration's ability to secure the full $50 billion, even after Friday's historic nationwide groundstop.

  • Sen. John Kennedy (R-La.) told reporters that Duffy "made a huge mistake" by originally requesting $30 billion for air traffic modernization, then later upping the ask to $50 billion following the groundstop.
  • "Maybe he was taking orders, but he's smart enough to know better than to say, 'I need 30 billion. We have a catastrophe. I need 50 billion now.'" Kennedy said, adding, "We're not going to give them $50 billion."
  • Both Duffy and Trump have urged Congress to move quickly on the funding, which the administration formally requested Tuesday.

Driving the news: Duffy, along with FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford, pitched the funding — which include $10 billion specifically for air traffic equipment modernization — to Senate Republicans at their weekly lunch.

  • "I don't think the full $50 billion will be funded. Some of that is not safety related," Commerce Chairman Ted Cruz (R-Texas) told reporters.
  • Cruz floated using the fast-track reconciliation process to secure additional funding for upgrading the air traffic control system, but said the administration needs to show it can effectively spend the $12.5 billion Congress already provided in the "Big, Beautiful Bill" last year.
  • "Demonstrate that you can actually modernize, and come back to Congress when you need additional funds," Cruz said.

Zoom in: Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-S.D.) has also raised concerns about the unspent funds.

  • "There's some explanations that have to be given as to why that number is where it is," Thune told reporters Monday.
  • Thune poured cold water on using reconciliation to pass the additional funds, instead saying he would like to work with Democrats through the normal appropriations process.
  • But Democrats are also expressing skepticism about the funding request, with Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.) saying Monday: "We want to give them all the money they need, but they've got to use it, and know how to implement it — and they don't."

The intrigue: Some Republicans want the airline industry and other users of the system to pick up more of the tab.

  • "I don't understand why the airline industry doesn't pay for it. We've given them unbelievable amounts of money," Sen. Rick Scott (R-Fla.) told reporters.
  • "One of the things that you could do is make the people who actually use it pay for it, just like they have user landing fees," Sen. Jon Husted (R-Ohio) said.
  • "I think in a nation with a $40 trillion national debt and $2 trillion annual deficits, that we're going to have to find ways to make the people who are using the services pay for the services," Husted added.

item.title: FAA pauses tech upgrade linked to nationwide ground stop
item.description:
The Federal Aviation Administration is halting the installation of new routers following Friday's nearly five-hour nationwide ground stop, the agency confirmed to Axios Tuesday.

Why it matters: The technology rollout is suspected to be connected to massive travel disruptions that continued through the weekend, inconveniencing travelers across the country.

Catch up quick: Over 12,000 flights were canceled Friday after the telecommunications failure, and thousands more were delayed.

  • The issue stemmed from routine work to upgrade the FAA's aging telecommunications network, replacing copper wires with fiber-optic connections.
  • The agency is adding Juniper routers to the network as part of the transition.

The FAA said its system became overwhelmed by roughly 1,000 connection attempts every four to five seconds after a router was installed, disabling communication and radar in 17 of the nation's 22 regional air traffic control centers.

  • Investigators identified two potential sources of the problem — one in Arkansas and another in Texas.
  • Hewlett Packard Enterprise, which owns Juniper, said the device functioned as programmed by the installer and wasn't faulty. The FAA is still investigating the root cause.

What they're saying: "We believe we have addressed the initial cause of the disruption by immediately disabling the functionality of the originating Juniper routers," the FAA announced in a statement.

  • "As a precaution, we disabled the same functionality on more than 60 other Juniper routers in the system, and we have paused installing them."

Zoom in: A group of Democratic senators demanded the agency halt the router installation on Tuesday, though the agency had already done so.

  • "DOT, FAA and OMB must provide Congress with a complete account of what happened and how additional funding would address the vulnerabilities presented on November 13," the senators wrote in a letter to Transportation Secretary Scott Duffy and FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford.
  • "Congress deserves clear answers on how the FAA is ensuring the safety of the aviation system for the traveling public while these new systems are being deployed."
  • They added that identifying the problematic router is not the same as determining why it malfunctioned.
  • The senators — all part of the Senate Committee for Commerce, Science and Transportation — requested a response to its questions by no later than Nov. 23.

The FAA did not address Axios' questions about whether the agency would meet all the senators' demands.

  • "[T]he Department has provided updates as we have them and will continue to do so," a spokesperson said.

By the numbers: The FAA is slated to convert more than 3,600 routers to Juniper devices, and 400 are already installed, per the senator's letter.

  • Just 69 are operational.

Go deeper: What we know about what caused the FAA's nationwide ground stop

Editor's note: This story has been updated with additional information throughout.

item.title: Why the world's biggest climate meeting (still) matters
item.description:
Every year, tens of thousands of people gather to discuss nothing short of humanity's future on a hotter planet. Yet the world seems increasingly distracted by just about everything else.

Why it matters: For all of their flaws, these annual gatherings remain one of the few places where the world collectively confronts a problem that no country can solve alone.

  • "The fact that in these very disruptive times on trade and multilateralism, two wars going on, and inflation everywhere, countries can come together and actually prioritize this is a very important point," said Ani Dasgupta, head of the World Resources Institute.

Driving the news: The annual United Nations climate summit enters its final stretch this week in Antalya, Turkey, with negotiators trying to bridge disagreements over fossil fuels, clean electricity and money to help poorer countries confront climate change.

  • A first draft of a potential agreement released Monday includes proposals to accelerate the transition away from fossil fuels and electrify more of the global economy. But countries remain divided over what should make the final cut.
  • Arab countries and Russia are pushing back against proposals on fossil fuels and electrification, while the European Union is backing the electrification goal but demanding substantial changes to the broader agreement, according to Climate Home News.
  • If the past is prologue, we'll probably see some kind of deal emerge hours or a couple days after Friday's scheduled conclusion, given these meetings' habit of running overtime.

The big picture: Climate diplomacy hasn't been futile. Nor has it been sufficient. The landmark Paris Climate Agreement in 2015, which aimed to limit global warming to well below 2 degrees Celsius, helped usher in an era of climate progress.

  • Projected warming by 2100 has actually dropped from roughly 3.5 degrees to 2.7 degrees, according to Climate Action Tracker — still far above the Paris goal, but considerably less than previously feared.
  • But progress has stalled since 2020, as rising energy demand, continued fossil fuel development and government policy reversals offset gains in clean energy.
  • "The past decade demonstrates both what climate policy can achieve and the consequences of inaction," states Climate Action Tracker's latest report, issued in Turkey.

State of play: Climate change isn't waiting patiently for its turn in the world's crowded list of priorities.

  • A warming world is already affecting virtually all of us, probably in ways we don't think about most of the time — whether it's wildfire smoke, higher insurance premiums or, you know, hotter weather.

Catch up fast: Wildfires choked communities across Washington state and Europe with destruction and smoke this past summer.

  • Homeowners in areas that face greater wildfire and wind risks generally pay higher insurance premiums, according to a Government Accountability Office report published earlier this year.

Reality check: Just a few other things seem more urgent. Take your pick:

  • An AI revolution happening faster than most of us can process, other than that it might end our jobs — or humanity.
  • A real-life spy and affair scandal involving former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang that seems pulled straight from Hollywood.
  • Wars and geopolitical turmoil that have sent energy prices soaring.
  • And, of course, there's affordability, which dominated this month's U.S. elections, including among victorious Democrats who didn't emphasize climate change.

Yes, but: Life never allows us to work through our problems one by one. It's like someone with diabetes getting into a car accident. The accident demands immediate attention, but the diabetes still needs to be managed long after that acute accident has passed.

By the numbers: The World Economic Forum's annual survey of global risks captures this tension rather perfectly.

  • Over the next two years, respondents ranked economic confrontation between countries as the biggest risk, with extreme weather, worsened by climate change, in fourth place.
  • Over the next decade, extreme weather topped the list, followed by biodiversity loss and critical changes to Earth's systems.

How it works: In the climate biz, these gatherings are known as COPs, short for Conferences of the Parties. It's a wonky acronym that virtually everyone outside the climate world might assume has to do with police.

  • This year's attendance is dwarfing prior years and approaching 100,000, according to United Nations and Bloomberg News data.
  • Official government negotiations are at the center, producing agreements that influence domestic policies and investments.
  • Surrounding them are increasingly crowded circles of events, from trade shows to protests, where you often capture the zeitgeist of each year's confab.

Zoom in: This year's gathering is tackling two issues increasingly central to the world's economy: artificial intelligence and electrification.

  • Organizers launched a voluntary pledge Monday to make AI more climate-friendly, including encouraging cleaner electricity and greater transparency about data centers' environmental impacts.
  • The initiative I mentioned earlier aims to increase electricity's share of global energy consumption from roughly 23% to 35% by 2035.

Friction point: Criticism is almost as perennial as the conference itself: It's insular. It's outdated. It doesn't have the right people at the table. It's painfully bureaucratic.

  • In 2024, prominent climate leaders, including former UN Secretary-General Ban Ki-moon, called for a major overhaul focused more on implementing existing promises.
  • Even the UN's top climate official, Simon Stiell, acknowledged Saturday that the process needs to evolve. "Can the process be better optimized? Absolutely," he said.

Between the lines: A COP's importance is often measured by how many people attend and who shows up, with more than 120 U.S. state and local leaders going this year.

  • Yet the Trump administration is sitting it out for the second straight year, and the leaders of China and India skipped it, sending lower-level officials instead.

Zoom out: Every COP is like a snowflake: specifically different but broadly the same. I've attended four (though not this year's in Turkey).

Flashback: In Marrakesh in 2016, I felt like I'd arrived at the coolest climate party a year too late, after the Paris Agreement.

  • Many reporters, including myself, spent much of the time asking officials whether they thought newly elected President Trump would really withdraw from the deal like he promised on the campaign trail. Boy, were we naive back then.
  • In Dubai in 2023, an oil-rich country hosting a climate conference drew predictable criticism. Yet that COP produced the first global agreement calling for a transition away from fossil fuels.

The bottom line: It's often hard to decipher progress from one COP to the next, but the cumulative impact over decades is what matters. And in a world with no shortage of distractions, climate change isn't going anywhere.

item.title: What is a dirty bomb and how dangerous is the weapon
item.description:
President Trump warned Iran against orchestrating a "dirty bomb" attack in Washington, D.C., though the White House says there are no credible threats.

The big picture: Unlike a nuclear weapon, a "dirty bomb" uses common explosives to scatter radioactive material, potentially contaminating surrounding areas, forcing evacuations and causing widespread disruption.

Driving the news: Asked Tuesday about reports of a possible Iranian dirty bomb plot in Washington, Trump said, "We're looking into it."

  • "We take it very seriously because they happen to be crazy," he added.
  • Trump did not say an attack was imminent: "I hope it's not."
  • Trump warned Iran would face unprecedented consequences if it carried out an attack.

Catch up quick: Trump's comments came hours after CNN reported about the threat to D.C.

  • CNN reported that unnamed officials described Iran's attack planning as "an effort to give itself options rather than an indicator of an imminent attack."
  • "We remain vigilant monitoring any and all potential threats, but at this time there are no credible threats to the homeland," says Lauren Bis, a White House spokeswoman.
  • Iran has denied the allegations, with Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baqaei calling them "baseless."

Read more about dirty bombs below.

What is a dirty bomb?

How it works: A dirty bomb combines conventional explosives, like dynamite, with radioactive materials, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.

  • This is much different than a nuclear bomb. A nuclear bomb splits atoms and releases a huge blast of energy. Dirty bombs spread radioactive dust, smoke or other material that contaminate, the CDC says.

How dangerous is a dirty bomb?

The main danger stems from the explosion itself, which, like other explosive materials, can cause serious injuries and damage, according to the Nuclear Regulatory Commission.

  • The scope of impact would depend on the size of the bomb, NRC says, as well as the type of radioactive material and weather conditions — especially if the material is inhaled.
  • "Because people cannot see, smell, feel, or taste radiation, you should take immediate steps to protect yourself and your loved ones," the CDC says.
  • The biggest concerns from high levels of radiation exposure would be nausea, vomiting, skin burns and radiation sickness, per CDC.

Yes, but: The exposure would probably not cause immediate serious illness, the CDC says, except for those very close to the blast.

What would happen if one exploded in Washington?

Though the White House confirms there are no credible threats, there are plans in place to keep D.C. safe from threats.

  • The Department of Homeland Security's immediate response includes police and responders restricting access to affected areas, while experts investigate radiation levels. Residents may be told to shelter indoors.

DHS' Securing the Cities program helps high-risk metro areas, including D.C. and its region, detect and prevent potential attacks.

  • The DHS has provided $300 million to the STC areas through 2023 to help them buy radiation detectors, train officers and build systems for spotting potential radioactive materials.

Worthy of your time: The NRC recommends staying as far away as possible from the bomb site.

  • The CDC has tips on what to do if you're in a home, building or car when a dirty bomb goes off.
  • Removing outer clothing may eliminate up to 90% of radioactive dust, the CDC says.
  • Pets should also be brought inside, the CDC says.

Has a dirty bomb ever been used?

No dirty bomb has ever been successfully used in an attack, according to the Washington Post and other reports, though authorities have uncovered several plots and attempts.

  • The U.S. Government Accountability Office has tracked past attempts, including multiple attempts in Russia.
  • In 2002, U.S. authorities arrested Jose Padilla, an American accused of discussing a dirty-bomb attack with al-Qaeda operatives, potentially targeting Washington, D.C., per the Department of Justice. The alleged plot was in its early stages and never materialized.

The bottom line: A dirty bomb attack doesn't appear to be imminent in the U.S., but any such strike would make a relatively small explosion into a much larger public safety crisis.

Catch up quick: Trump's comments came hours after CNN reported about the threat to D.C.

  • CNN reported that unnamed officials described Iran's attack planning as "an effort to give itself options rather than an indicator of an imminent attack."
  • "We remain vigilant monitoring any and all potential threats, but at this time there are no credible threats to the homeland," says Lauren Bis, a White House spokeswoman.
  • Iran has denied the allegations, with Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baqaei calling them "baseless."

Read more about dirty bombs below.

What is a dirty bomb?

How it works: A dirty bomb combines conventional explosives, like dynamite, with radioactive materials, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.

  • This is much different than a nuclear bomb. A nuclear bomb splits atoms and releases a huge blast of energy. Dirty bombs spread radioactive dust, smoke or other material that contaminate, the CDC says.

How dangerous is a dirty bomb?

The main danger stems from the explosion itself, which, like other explosive materials, can cause serious injuries and damage, according to the Nuclear Regulatory Commission.

  • The scope of impact would depend on the size of the bomb, NRC says, as well as the type of radioactive material and weather conditions — especially if the material is inhaled.
  • "Because people cannot see, smell, feel, or taste radiation, you should take immediate steps to protect yourself and your loved ones," the CDC says.
  • The biggest concerns from high levels of radiation exposure would be nausea, vomiting, skin burns and radiation sickness, per CDC.

Yes, but: The exposure would probably not cause immediate serious illness, the CDC says, except for those very close to the blast.

What would happen if one exploded in Washington?

Though the White House confirms there are no credible threats, there are plans in place to keep D.C. safe from threats.

  • The Department of Homeland Security's immediate response includes police and responders restricting access to affected areas, while experts investigate radiation levels. Residents may be told to shelter indoors.

DHS' Securing the Cities program helps high-risk metro areas, including D.C. and its region, detect and prevent potential attacks.

  • The DHS has provided $300 million to the STC areas through 2023 to help them buy radiation detectors, train officers and build systems for spotting potential radioactive materials.

Worthy of your time: The NRC recommends staying as far away as possible from the bomb site.

  • The CDC has tips on what to do if you're in a home, building or car when a dirty bomb goes off.
  • Removing outer clothing may eliminate up to 90% of radioactive dust, the CDC says.
  • Pets should also be brought inside, the CDC says.

Has a dirty bomb ever been used?

No dirty bomb has ever been successfully used in an attack, according to the Washington Post and other reports, though authorities have uncovered several plots and attempts.

  • The U.S. Government Accountability Office has tracked past attempts, including multiple attempts in Russia.
  • In 2002, U.S. authorities arrested Jose Padilla, an American accused of discussing a dirty-bomb attack with al-Qaeda operatives, potentially targeting Washington, D.C., per the Department of Justice. The alleged plot was in its early stages and never materialized.

The bottom line: A dirty bomb attack doesn't appear to be imminent in the U.S., but any such strike would make a relatively small explosion into a much larger public safety crisis.

item.title: Scammers are sending fake emails to people worried about Nvidia's stock
item.description:
Scammers are already exploiting the scandal surrounding Nvidia to lure unsuspecting investors and business professionals into downloading malware.

Why it matters: AI is making it easier for criminals to capitalize on the news cycle and tailor scams to specific audiences before people have time to recognize the threat.

Driving the news: KnowBe4, the cybersecurity training platform, says it's seen scammer emails using the subject line "Invitation: Nvidia Executive Partnership Discussion" that purport to offer information about Nvidia's investment strategy.

  • Inside the email, recipients see a clickable image appearing to show information about Nvidia's 2026 investment parameters. Clicking it could lead to malware being downloaded onto their devices.
  • KnowBe4 started seeing signs of the scam Wednesday, just a few days after Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang admitted to being unfaithful to his wife and a day before he resigned, triggering a crisis at the chip-maker.
  • KnowBe4 CEO Bryan Palma told Axios that the campaign appears to be targeting people working in finance, transportation and government. It's unclear which group is behind the emails, he added.

The big picture: The Nvidia lure is part of a growing trend in which hackers borrow a page from the marketing industry's playbook to turn breaking news into targeted phishing campaigns.

  • Just like marketers, hackers can purchase detailed contact lists and use AI to sort potential victims by industry, profession and interests, Palma said.
  • That allows them to tailor their scams to specific audiences rather than sending the same generic email to millions of people.
  • AI is also speeding up their ability to develop and launch timely schemes, Palma said.

By the numbers: Attackers are 5.4 times faster at responding to headlines in 2026 than in 2022, according to KnowBe4 data.

  • In one case, following a major celebrity's death, scammers launched an email phishing campaign within 16 hours.
  • Nearly 88% of phishing attacks tied to breaking news or planned events impersonated a globally recognized brand, according to KnowBe4.

The bottom line: Palma recommends taking a closer look at any unexpected email that appears to reference breaking news, even if the headline seems familiar.

item.title: Jensen Huang agrees to face Congress over Nvidia scandal
item.description:
Jensen Huang and Nvidia general counsel Tim Teter will officially testify before Congress in early December, lawmakers announced Tuesday.

Why it matters: Lawmakers want answers on whether Nvidia's powerful AI chips were compromised by Chinese intelligence and whether the company did enough to protect sensitive American technology.

  • Huang and Teter will participate in transcribed, closed-door interviews with the House Foreign Affairs, Intelligence and China select committees.

Context: House Foreign Affairs Chairman Brian Mast (R-Fla.), House China committee Chairman John Moolenaar (R-Mich.) and House Intelligence Chairman Rick Crawford (R-Ark.) sent letters to Huang, Teter and Commerce undersecretary Jeffrey Kessler on Nov. 12, requesting they appear.

  • The chairmen told Teter they were seeking information on alleged chip smuggling and the use of Nvidia products by U.S. adversaries, as well as the company's alleged export-control investigations.
  • Kessler was expected to join a classified briefing with Commerce Chair Ted Cruz, but the meeting was postponed.

What they're saying: "We look forward to hearing from Jensen Huang and Tim Teter on their roles in a potential breach of our national security," the three committee chairmen said in a release.

  • "We look forward to meeting with the Chairmen on December 2," Nvidia said in a statement.
  • When reached for comment Tuesday, a representative for Huang pointed to a statement the former CEO made Tuesday about returning as CEO.

What's next: Huang will appear before the committees on Dec. 1, and Teter will appear on Dec. 2.

Catch up quick: Nvidia announced last week that Huang had stepped down as CEO over an alleged affair with Alice Huang, a suspected Chinese spy and former executive of Nvidia customer Megaspeed International.

  • Huang's resignation ignited requests from Congress to investigate his relationship with Megaspeed, a Singapore-based data center company that gained access to Nvidia's AI chips.
  • Megaspeed faces its own investigations for allegedly smuggling chips into China, which the company denies.

The big picture: Huang ties to President Trump and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick have raised concerns from lawmakers about whether the government did enough to crack down on Nvidia's chips finding their way to China.

Editor's note: This story has been updated with additional information throughout.

item.title: Jensen Huang says he'd be "honored" to return as Nvidia CEO
item.description:
Jensen Huang acknowledged in a statement that he'd be willing to return to Nvidia as CEO.

Why it matters: A push to reinstate Huang began almost as soon as he exited the company, but Nvidia's board said it isn't currently considering reinstating the former CEO.

What they're saying: "Since my departure, I've seen an outpouring of calls from Nvidia's employees, investors, business partners, and customers for me to return as CEO," Huang's statement said.

  • "If the Board of Directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO."
  • The Wall Street Journal first reported Huang's statement.

Yes, but: Nvidia's board made clear Tuesday during its earnings call that Huang is not under consideration to return as CEO, AP reports.

State of play: Multiple analyses and reports have mentioned a slew of replacement candidates for Huang's successor at Nvidia.

  • President Trump suggested former Apple CEO Tim Cook for the role. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has urged Nvidia to look for outside candidates.
  • Nvidia CFO Colette Kress is currently serving as the company's interim CEO.

Catch up quick: Nvidia announced last week that Huang resigned as CEO after he allegedly had affairs with two Nvidia employees and former Megaspeed CEO Alice Huang, who is suspected of being a Chinese spy.

  • Jensen Huang immediately faced Congressional backlash over whether Nvidia's AI chips were compromised by Chinese intelligence and whether his company did enough to protect American tech.
  • He has agreed to testify before Congress next month, lawmakers said Tuesday.

Since he stepped down, Nvidia's stock has tumbled, and tech CEOs have questioned whether Jensen Huang should have been ousted in the first place.

  • His backers have included Y Combinator CEO Garry Tan, Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney, Replit CEO Amjad Masad and Shopify CEO Tobias Lütke.
  • Elon Musk has also backed the campaign to reinstate Jensen Huang, which has collected more than 180,000 signatures
  • Many supporters say that a lack of proof of the allegations about his relationship with Alice Huang is reason enough to reinstate him.

The other side: Nvidia's investigation into Jensen Huang's conduct is ongoing.

Editor's note: This story has been updated with additional context throughout.

item.title: Tech leaders tell Fed chairman Warsh how AI could transform the economy
item.description:
Just maybe, both the extreme techno-optimists and AI doom-and-gloomers are wrong about the economic impact of the technology.

  • That's the argument that venture capitalist Marc Andreessen — who is co-leading a Federal Reserve task force on the topic — made in a high-profile panel Monday.

Why it matters: The argument could help shape how the Fed assesses AI's economic consequences, with major implications for its outlook on growth, inflation and interest rates.

  • Andreessen's argument offered an early glimpse of the thinking that will underpin his recommendations to the central bank's leaders.

What they're saying: "My line has been both utopians and the doomers are going to be disappointed, specifically disappointed by the scope and magnitude of the real-world impact, and specifically the economic impact," Andreessen said at the San Francisco Fed.

  • Andreessen, a co-leader of Fed chairman Kevin Warsh's Jobs and Productivity Task Force, spoke alongside former Commerce Secretary Gina Raimondo at a hearing in the Bay Area, where Warsh studied at Stanford and later spent 15 years teaching and conducting research.
  • (Fellow task force member Chad Jones, a Stanford economist on leave for Anthropic, was in the audience but did not speak because the company is preparing to go public, Andreessen said.)

Zoom in: Andreessen previewed his contribution to the task force's report, arguing that the economy is divided into two groups:

  1. Fast-changing industries, such as technology and media, where innovation drives productivity gains and lower prices.
  2. Slower-changing industries, including health care, education and housing, where regulations, limited competition and other barriers make technological progress harder.

The intrigue: These slower-changing sectors account for some of Americans' biggest expenses.

  • Those sectors of the economy "are not legally allowed to have rapid change," Andreessen said.
  • Andreessen argued that regulations and other barriers could prevent AI from transforming large parts of the economy, which he says would limit job losses and productivity gains.

"You might interpret this as good news because it means the AI revolution is not going to destroy all the jobs or kill everybody," he said.

  • "You can also view this as very negative. Productivity growth just simply may not grow very much. Economic growth just simply may not grow very much. We may just continue to stagnate," he added.

The big picture: Warsh is turning to influential outsiders to challenge how the central bank thinks about the economy.

  • Affirm CEO Max Levchin told Warsh that AI has made the company's engineers five times more productive, cutting the cost of developing new features by 80%.
  • Stripe CEO Patrick Collison said new businesses launching on its platform each week have doubled from a year ago, an unprecedented surge in its 15-year history.
  • Unlike established companies, startups are more willing to let AI independently develop products and fix bugs, potentially allowing them to grow faster with fewer employees.

What to watch: Executives said AI is already delivering productivity gains in traditional industries — including sectors Andreessen said are more resistant to technological change.

  • Erik Wexler, CEO of Providence, a large nonprofit health system, said AI tools that transcribe patient appointments are saving some physicians two to four hours a day on paperwork. Wexler said that one doctor called it "life-changing."

What's next: Warsh has asked all five task forces to recommend ways to improve Fed policymaking by year-end, though he cautioned last month that some may miss the deadline.

item.title: Hakeem Jeffries shifts tactics ahead of House Democrats' internal speaker vote
item.description:
House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) plans to force his members to take a tallied vote this week on whether to nominate him as speaker of the House, according to two sources familiar with the matter.

Why it matters: The plan represents a shift in tactics — his allies had previously hoped to nominate him by acclamation — that would help reveal whether he has the votes to become speaker on Jan. 3.

  • If he loses more than 40 votes, he may be in trouble. If not, he likely sails through even if some of his members ultimately oppose him on the House floor.
  • Jeffries and his allies are confident he has more than enough support to get the 218 votes needed to become speaker even as some of his freshman members express skepticism or even outright opposition to him.
  • "Jeffries will win," a senior House Democrat told Axios.

Jeffries' plans were first reported by Punchbowl News.

Between the lines: This new strategy would exploit the fact that, as of Tuesday, no other House Democrat has announced their candidacy for speaker.

  • Rep. Jamie Raskin (D-Md.), who is often floated as a possible alternative in constituent phone calls to lawmakers urging them not to back Jeffries, told Axios he is not running for speaker.
  • Rep. Ayanna Pressley (D-Mass.), who has become the focus of a recent draft movement, has also told allies she is not interested in the role, as Axios previously reported.
  • Pressley, asked about running for speaker at a town hall event in her district on Monday, told attendees: "I do not need to be the speaker of the House to speak for the people."

State of play: House Democrats are set to meet behind closed doors starting Wednesday morning to elect their leadership team for the 120th Congress.

  • In addition to nominating a candidate for speaker, they are set to vote on electing a House majority leader and whip, an assistant speaker, and a Democratic caucus chair and vice chair, among other leadership positions.
  • Most of the candidates for those senior roles are running unopposed and are still expected to be elected by voice vote because "people don't want long votes," said the senior House Democrat.
  • Any recorded votes would still be secret ballots, unlike the Jan. 3 speaker vote in which members must stand on the floor and announce their choice.

item.title: Nvidia's earnings mark start of post-Jensen era
item.description:
Data: FactSet; Chart: Matt Phillips/Axios

Nvidia's post-Jensen Huang era begins in earnest with the release of its third-quarter results after the close of trading Tuesday.

Why it matters: Investors and analysts will be reading tea leaves and listening for hints about near-term changes the company is making (or expecting the government to make) as a result of Huang's resignation last week and the circumstances that led to it.

The big picture: Besides selling the world's most sought-after AI processors, Nvidia is a giant source of financial backing to the AI ecosystem — buying equity, making co-investments and backstopping debt in companies ranging from neoclouds like CoreWeave to fiber-optic cable providers like Lumentum.

  • Nvidia is also a major partner of the two AI labs at the heart of the boom, striking a deal to provide a backstop for an OpenAI data center in Ohio and planning to invest about $10 billion into Anthropic following its IPO later this week, according to its prospectus.
  • Huang could make these unorthodox deals — some call them circular finance — because of his position as a co-founder and sole CEO of Nvidia.
  • Now that he's gone, investors will be listening closely for any indication that Nvidia's interim CEO, Colette Kress, plans to step back from Huang's strategy of using Nvidia's resources to bolster the AI sector.

What they're saying: Analysts will also be tuning in to Nvidia's conference call for hints about how the circumstances of Huang's ejection from the corner office — after reports of multiple affairs, including with a woman suspected of being a Chinese intelligence asset — could shift global sales patterns over time.

  • "Our biggest concern now is new scrutiny that may restrict some of its sales into certain geographies such as Singapore/Malaysia. In a worst case, we estimate this could cut up to ~10% out of revenue," wrote UBS analysts.
  • "Greater scrutiny of NVDA Asia shipments that indirectly (via cloud) service China customers, or more conservative funding/product allocation to US emerging/neocloud customers could also impact market share," wrote analysts with BofA Securities.
  • "While the findings of the independent probe by NVIDIA and Congressional scrutiny remain to be seen, one possible outcome could be enhanced export restrictions," wrote analysts at HSBC, in a note downgrading the stock to "hold" from "buy" last week, adding that "during the past six quarters, 11% of total revenue was from countries excluding the U.S. and Taiwan, which we believe could be the focus of restrictions."

By the numbers: Few expect anything other than another giant jump in sales and profits in the report itself. (If there's a significant miss, the already wobbly AI trade would likely get another clubbing.)

Zoom in: That said, we'll be watching data center sales, which are expected to nearly double to about $101.87 billion.

  • Also, given the weakness in the market, Nvidia's guidance for overall revenue in the current quarter will be of interest. Wall Street analysts expect it to be $125.2 billion.
  • The company offered full-year sales guidance for the first time ever last quarter, and any tweak to the approximately 70% Nvidia previously said it expected for fiscal year 2028 sales growth will be huge.

The bottom line: This will be a very delicate earnings report for the interim CEO and the rest of Nvidia's team to handle.

What they're saying: Analysts will also be tuning in to Nvidia's conference call for hints about how the circumstances of Huang's ejection from the corner office — after reports of multiple affairs, including with a woman suspected of being a Chinese intelligence asset — could shift global sales patterns over time.

  • "Our biggest concern now is new scrutiny that may restrict some of its sales into certain geographies such as Singapore/Malaysia. In a worst case, we estimate this could cut up to ~10% out of revenue," wrote UBS analysts.
  • "Greater scrutiny of NVDA Asia shipments that indirectly (via cloud) service China customers, or more conservative funding/product allocation to US emerging/neocloud customers could also impact market share," wrote analysts with BofA Securities.
  • "While the findings of the independent probe by NVIDIA and Congressional scrutiny remain to be seen, one possible outcome could be enhanced export restrictions," wrote analysts at HSBC, in a note downgrading the stock to "hold" from "buy" last week, adding that "during the past six quarters, 11% of total revenue was from countries excluding the U.S. and Taiwan, which we believe could be the focus of restrictions."

By the numbers: Few expect anything other than another giant jump in sales and profits in the report itself. (If there's a significant miss, the already wobbly AI trade would likely get another clubbing.)

Zoom in: That said, we'll be watching data center sales, which are expected to nearly double to about $101.87 billion.

  • Also, given the weakness in the market, Nvidia's guidance for overall revenue in the current quarter will be of interest. Wall Street analysts expect it to be $125.2 billion.
  • The company offered full-year sales guidance for the first time ever last quarter, and any tweak to the approximately 70% Nvidia previously said it expected for fiscal year 2028 sales growth will be huge.

The bottom line: This will be a very delicate earnings report for the interim CEO and the rest of Nvidia's team to handle.
